social.neighborhoodNote: Eviction filings -- a downstream proxy for housing precarity where vacancy/burden data is thin at fine geography -- are heavily concentrated in the Bronx: in 2024 the eight community districts with the highest eviction filing rates citywide were all in the Bronx (Morrisania/Crotona highest at 159.7 per 1,000 rental units), with the ninth-highest in the Rockaways, Queens; Stuyvesant Town/Turtle Bay in Manhattan had the lowest measured rate (12.7 per 1,000). Severe rent burden at neighbourhood level ranges from 21.6% in the Financial District to 37.6% in Mott Haven/Melrose. Source: NYU Furman Center, State of Renters and Their Homes 2024, using NYS Office of Court Administration eviction filing data. The Furman report could not be fetched directly (403 Forbidden on both www and non-www domains); its figures here are recovered from search indexing of the report and are held at medium confidence.

subIndicators.name: Renter households rent-burdened (30%+ of income) and severely rent-burdened (50%+), citywide and by borough -- ACS basis
subIndicators.value: Citywide 2023 (ACS basis, all renter households): just over half rent-burdened -- 28.9% severely burdened and 23.0% moderately burdened, both down slightly from 2013 (29.6% and 24.4%). Severely rent-burdened share by borough: Bronx 35.8%, Staten Island 32.1%, Brooklyn 28.1%, Queens 28.0%, Manhattan 25.4%. NOTE ON BASIS: these are ACS-derived figures reported by the Furman Center, covering ALL renter households. They are not comparable to NYCHVS burden figures, which exclude households in public housing or with vouchers -- on that restricted NYCHVS basis, severe burden runs 22-28% by race of householder and no group exceeds 47% total burden. The two bases must not be merged.
subIndicators.source: NYU Furman Center, State of Renters and Their Homes 2024 (ACS-based)
subIndicators.note: Source not directly fetchable (403); figures recovered via search indexing. The Staten Island 32.1% figure specifically was not recovered on re-verification and should be re-confirmed in Phase 2.

subIndicators.name: Rent burden by race/ethnicity and income of householder, NYCHVS basis (equity disaggregation)
subIndicators.value: Severely rent burdened (>50% of income), 2023, renter households NOT in means-tested housing: Black non-Hispanic-headed 28%, Hispanic-headed 27%, Asian non-Hispanic-headed 26%, White non-Hispanic-headed 22%. Total burden (>30%) is highest for Black-headed households at 47% and Hispanic-headed at 45%. Foreign-born-headed households: 27% severely, 19% moderately. Households with one or more older adult, one or more person with a disability, or a single person: ~35% severely burdened plus ~20% moderately. By income: among renter households earning under $25,000 outside means-tested housing, 86% were severely rent burdened and 4% moderately (85%/7% in 2021); $25,000-$49,999: 45% severely, 36% moderately; $50,000-$99,999: 10% severely, 33% moderately. IMPORTANT: NYCHVS excludes households in public housing and households reporting a voucher from its rent-burden analysis entirely -- it publishes NO voucher-household burden rate, and the 86%/85% figures above belong to low-income households WITHOUT vouchers or public housing.
subIndicators.source: NYC HPD, 2023 NYCHVS Selected Initial Findings, Table 18 and narrative

subIndicators.name: DHS/HPD shelter census and record system-wide use
subIndicators.value: 87,442 people slept in DHS+HPD shelters in May 2026 (18,890 families and 29,008 single adults), up from 73,219 in Dec 2024 and 65,640 in Dec 2023. Across all NYC shelters, ~96,500 people were sheltered nightly in April 2026, 65% of them family members including 30,955 children. A record 194,531 unique individuals used the DHS shelter system at some point during 2025 -- the most in the system's history. Coalition for the Homeless counts more than 350,000 New Yorkers without homes as of 1 January 2026, and finds the number of longer-term New Yorkers sleeping in DHS shelters nightly rose 27% (+12,442 people) over the four years of the Adams administration. Separately, the asylum-seeker shelter population peaked at ~70,000 (Jan 2024) and had fallen to ~33,300 by 28 Sept 2025 (-51%), after more than 239,200 asylum seekers had entered the shelter system cumulatively since spring 2022 -- so the record domestic shelter use above was reached as the asylum surge receded, not because of it.
subIndicators.source: Coalition for the Homeless, State of the Homeless 2026 and DHS/HPD shelter census tracker; NYC Comptroller, Asylum Seeker Census
subIndicators.note: Asylum-seeker figures held at medium confidence: the Comptroller's Asylum Seeker Census page returns 403 to direct fetch and its figures were recovered via search indexing.

subIndicators.name: NYCHA scale and capital need
subIndicators.value: NYCHA provides housing to 511,384 authorized residents in over 177,565 apartments across 335 developments, through conventional public housing, Section 8 and PACT/RAD combined (Fact Sheet, released January 2025). Components: 298,206 residents in 152,926 apartments across 243 developments in conventional public housing (Section 9); 46,455 residents in 24,639 apartments across 92 developments converted under PACT/RAD; 107,979 families (223,114 authorized residents) assisted through Section 8. NYCHA public housing and Section 8 together occupy 10.9% of the city's rental apartments and house 6.2% of NYC's population; average public-housing family income is $26,129 and average monthly rent $621. The 2023 Physical Needs Assessment found $78.3B in 20-year capital repair needs across the 264 directly-managed properties (161,400 apartments), up 73% from $45.3B in the 2017 PNA, with $57.8B (74%) in apartments, heating systems, building exteriors and plumbing; the next PNA is slated for 2028, and NYCHA's Jan-2025 Fact Sheet characterises the backlog as 'nearly $80 billion'. NYCHA's Section 8 voucher waitlist reopened in June 2024 for the first time since 10 Dec 2009: 633,808 households applied, of which 200,000 were selected by lottery.
subIndicators.source: NYCHA Fact Sheet (released January 2025); NYCHA 2023 Physical Needs Assessment; NYCHA press release 2024-08-01

subIndicators.name: NYCHA public housing by borough
subIndicators.value: Bronx: 63 developments, 37,544 apartments, 75,783 residents. Brooklyn: 64 developments, 47,725 apartments, 94,553 residents. Manhattan: 77 developments, 48,284 apartments, 91,010 residents. Queens: 21 developments, 15,348 apartments, 29,530 residents. Staten Island: 8 developments, 3,876 apartments, 7,330 residents. (Conventional public housing only; excludes PACT/RAD-converted developments and Section 8.)
subIndicators.source: NYCHA Fact Sheet (released January 2025), Public Housing Borough Breakdown

subIndicators.name: Rent-stabilized stock and Rent Guidelines Board action
subIndicators.value: 996,600 rent-stabilized units in 2023 -- 27% of NYC's overall housing stock and 41% of all rental units, of which about 76% (758,700 units) are stabilized via the Emergency Tenant Protection Act. Alongside these sit 24,020 rent-controlled units, 1,139,000 market rentals, 178,700 public housing units and 52,810 rentals regulated in some other way. For Oct 2025-Sept 2026 leases the RGB approved +3% (1-yr) / +4.5% (2-yr). On 25 June 2026, in a 7-1 vote, the RGB approved a 0%/0% rent freeze for both 1-year and 2-year renewals beginning 1 Oct 2026 through 30 Sept 2027 -- the first-ever freeze on 2-year leases and Mayor Mamdani's signature campaign pledge fulfilled six months into his term. A pro-landlord board member resigned in protest hours before the final vote.
subIndicators.source: NYC HPD, 2023 NYCHVS Selected Initial Findings (stock counts); NYC Rent Guidelines Board; contemporaneous coverage of the 25 June 2026 RGB vote (amNewYork, Commercial Observer, Brownstoner)

subIndicators.name: Eviction filings, citywide and by borough (per 1,000 rental units, 2024)
subIndicators.value: 119,646 new eviction filings citywide in 2024, down 9.6% from 2023 and still well below pre-pandemic levels though above the 2020-2022 pandemic years. Filing rate per 1,000 rental units by borough (2024): Bronx 104.1, Queens 47.1, Brooklyn 45.2, Staten Island 42.9, Manhattan 36.6.
subIndicators.source: NYU Furman Center, State of Renters and Their Homes 2024, using NYS Office of Court Administration Universal Case Management System data
subIndicators.note: Source not directly fetchable (403); figures recovered via search indexing of the report. Coalition for the Homeless separately reports a rising eviction series (42,110 in 2021 to 114,821 in 2025) on a definition that does not reconcile cleanly with Furman's filing counts; the two series should not be compared without resolving the definitions in Phase 2.

subIndicators.name: Right to Counsel representation rate, citywide and Bronx
subIndicators.value: Attorney representation for eligible tenants facing eviction fell from 71% (Q4 FY2021) to 42% (Q4 FY2024) citywide, and further to 30% by March 2025. In the Bronx, where evictions are most concentrated, representation fell from 81% (Q4 2021) to 31% (Q4 2024). The full-representation caseload providers were expected to carry grew 51% from FY2019 to FY2024 (approximately 16,300 to 24,500 households), while demand for brief legal services grew 475% over the same period. Where full representation was secured, 89% of tenants remained stably housed (FY2024); across 2018-2023, 81% of represented households avoided eviction (34,571 of 41,161 cases). Providers estimate the City would need to more than double its spending to meet demand; advocates have called for $350M annually.
subIndicators.source: NYC Comptroller, 'Evictions Up, Representation Down' (May 2025)

subIndicators.name: Illegal/basement apartments and Hurricane Ida
subIndicators.value: 11 of the 13 Hurricane Ida-related deaths in NYC (1 Sept 2021) were drownings in basement apartments, mostly of immigrants; DOB found 5 of the 6 apartments where deaths occurred were illegally converted. Against an estimated 100,000+ illegal basement/cellar units citywide, the legalization record is close to nil: the Basement Apartment Conversion Pilot Program (BACPP), launched in 2019 in Brooklyn Community District 5, drew just 5 active participants out of roughly 8,000 homeowners contacted, against an initial goal of 40 units, and NO participant had completed a conversion as of mid-2025 -- blocked by the State Multiple Dwelling Law, accessibility mandates, cost and unforeseen physical non-compliances. A new citywide pilot mandated by Local Law 126 of 2024 (part of City of Yes for Housing Opportunity) is the current pathway: DOB/HPD published proposed rules in November 2025, eligibility is limited to apartments that existed before 20 April 2024 in named community districts with basic safety features, owners have until 20 April 2029 to apply and 10 years to reach full compliance. Critically, properties in flood-prone areas are categorically ineligible -- excluding the very exposure that killed 11 people in 2021.
subIndicators.source: ABC News and NBC New York coverage of Ida deaths and DOB findings; CHPC, Basement Apartment Conversion Pilot Program Final Report; NYC HPD/DOB press release 074-25 on the Local Law 126 of 2024 pilot rules

subIndicators.name: Housing quality: HPD violations and Worst Landlord Watchlist
subIndicators.value: NYC Public Advocate's 2025 Worst Landlord Watchlist: top-ranked Margaret Brunn held 4,872 open HPD violations across 24 buildings and second-ranked Donald Hastings held 3,889 across 36 buildings -- both linked to A&E Real Estate Holdings, together 60 buildings and roughly 8,761 open violations, more than any prior top two in the list's history. Violations cited include heat and hot-water outages, rodent infestation and collapsing infrastructure. A&E states it has invested over $800M across its portfolio since acquisition and cleared 35,000 violations; the City separately won a $2.1M settlement against A&E to correct violations at an Upper West Side building. Separately, NYCHVS 2023 found housing-quality problems reported in 43% of public housing units against 10% of market rentals.
subIndicators.source: NYC Public Advocate Jumaane Williams, Worst Landlord Watchlist 2025; NYC HPD, 2023 NYCHVS Selected Initial Findings

subIndicators.name: Median asking rent by borough (derived, stale)
subIndicators.value: DERIVED FIGURE, NOT A PUBLISHED MEDIAN: quarterly averages of monthly StreetEasy median asking rents for Q1 2025, as reported in secondary market-trend aggregation -- Manhattan ~$4,392, Brooklyn ~$3,480, Queens ~$3,000, Bronx ~$2,821, Staten Island ~$2,679. Secondary reporting also indicates Manhattan's median reached ~$4,720-4,995/month and Brooklyn's ~$4,000 by late 2025 (Douglas Elliman/Miller Samuel). None of these were confirmed against a primary StreetEasy or Miller Samuel table, and all are 15+ months stale at the time of review. For a primary, published rent figure use NYCHVS 2023 instead: median monthly contract rent for all renter-occupied units $1,641 citywide, $1,500 among rent-stabilized units, $1,740 in Queens and $1,600 in Staten Island.
subIndicators.source: StreetEasy market data via secondary aggregation; Douglas Elliman/Miller Samuel Rental Report (Nov 2025); NYC HPD 2023 NYCHVS for the primary median contract rent

subIndicators.name: 485-x and Good Cause Eviction, statewide adoption
subIndicators.value: 485-x ('Affordable Neighborhoods for New Yorkers') replaced the expired 421-a tax incentive, adopted 20 April 2024, requiring permanently affordable units on a sliding scale: 25% at a weighted average 80% AMI for rental projects of 100+ units (35-year benefit), 25% at 60% AMI for very large projects of 150+ units in Zones A/B (40-year benefit), 20% at 80% AMI for projects of 6-99 units (35-year benefit), with restricted units permanently rent stabilized and construction wage floors from $40/hour up to $72.45/hour by zone and project size. Good Cause Eviction took effect 20 April 2024 in NYC by default (rent-increase caps and just-cause eviction protections for most market-rate tenants below roughly 345% of Fair Market Rent); 17 NY municipalities have since opted in, and approximately 1 million renters statewide are now covered.
subIndicators.source: NYC HPD 485-x program page; NY State Senate press release on Good Cause adoption

global.levelRationale: Scored on the two things that are actually quantified plus the direction of policy. MAGNITUDE (pulls the score down from 'critical'): the primary, published measure of housing withheld from the market -- units held for seasonal, recreational or occasional use, the NYCHVS category that contains pieds-a-terre and dedicated short-term rentals -- is 58,810 units in 2023, about 1.6% of a 3,705,000-unit stock, and it FELL 43% from 102,900 in 2021 (74,950 in 2017). The State's own estimate of units above the new pied-a-terre tax thresholds is ~14,000, with a DOF-derived Comptroller sample of 19,107 properties of which 17,125 are in Manhattan. Blackstone and Ivanhoe Cambridge hold 11,200 units at Stuyvesant Town-Peter Cooper Village. Those are real transmission-channel quantities, and they are modest and shrinking. TRANSPARENCY (pulls the score up): the anti-anonymity regime has been dismantled at both federal and state level within 12 months -- FinCEN's March-2025 interim final rule removed roughly 99.8% of entities from Corporate Transparency Act beneficial-ownership reporting by exempting all US-formed entities; the residential real estate GTOs expired 28 Feb 2026; their nationwide replacement rule took effect 1 March 2026 and was vacated by the U.S. District Court for E.D. Texas on 19 March 2026 (on appeal), so no federal shell-company residential reporting requirement is in force; and New York's own LLC Transparency Act, effective 1 Jan 2026, was narrowed by the Governor's 19 Dec 2025 veto of S8432 to reach only non-US-formed LLCs, so the state does not backstop the federal gap. That is the weakest disclosure posture since the GTOs began in 2016. COUNTERWEIGHT: New York State enacted a pied-a-terre surcharge on 26 May 2026, effective 1 July 2026 -- the first binding fiscal instrument against non-primary-residence ownership after roughly seven years of failed proposals. Net: a real and worsening opacity problem attached to a measured channel of modest and declining magnitude, with a new tool just switched on. 60 -- above 'needs attention', clearly short of 'critical'. The previous level of 100 rested on an unverifiable '~10% of Manhattan condo transactions' figure that has been removed, and cannot be sustained without it. Confidence medium: the transparency findings are firm, the magnitude figures are firm, but no source quantifies the share of NYC purchases made by foreign nationals or anonymous entities.
global.indicator: NYC housing withheld from the market for non-primary-residence and occasional use, and the visibility of global and anonymous capital in NYC housing
global.value: PRIMARY QUANTIFICATION: 58,810 NYC housing units were held for seasonal, recreational or occasional use in 2023 -- 26% of all units vacant but not available for rent or sale, the single largest such category -- down from 102,900 in 2021 and 74,950 in 2017 (2023 NYCHVS). New York State enacted a pied-a-terre surcharge on 26 May 2026 in the FY2026-27 Budget Bill, effective 1 July 2026 and sunsetting 30 June 2031, taxing non-primary residences at 4.0-6.5% for Class 2 condos and co-ops above $1M and 0.8-1.3% for Class 1 homes above $5M in Phase 1; the State estimates ~14,000 NYC apartments and homes fall in scope, and the Comptroller's DOF-based analysis identified 19,107 properties of which 17,125 are in Manhattan, with revenue revised to $340-380M from an initial $500M. TRANSPARENCY REGIME, as of July 2026: FinCEN's residential real estate Geographic Targeting Orders -- which required title insurers to identify the natural persons behind shell-company, non-financed purchases over $300,000 in covered metros including NYC -- were last renewed effective 10 Oct 2025 and expired 28 Feb 2026. Their nationwide replacement, the Residential Real Estate Rule (finalized Aug 2024, delayed from 1 Dec 2025), took effect 1 March 2026 and was VACATED by the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Texas on 19 March 2026; FinCEN states reporting persons need not file and face no liability for not filing, and FinCEN and DOJ have appealed. Separately, FinCEN's interim final rule of 21 March 2025 (effective 26 March 2025) exempted all US-formed entities -- including the LLCs typically used to hold anonymous NYC real estate -- from Corporate Transparency Act beneficial-ownership reporting, removing roughly 99.8% of originally covered entities; a final rule reached OIRA on 5 June 2026 and remains unpublished. New York's own LLC Transparency Act took effect 1 Jan 2026 but, after the Governor's 19 Dec 2025 veto of S8432, reaches only LLCs formed outside the United States, exempting domestic LLCs. INSTITUTIONAL OWNERSHIP: Blackstone (headquartered in Manhattan) and Ivanhoe Cambridge -- a subsidiary of Caisse de depot et placement du Quebec, a Quebec public pension fund -- have owned Stuyvesant Town-Peter Cooper Village (11,200 apartments, ~30,000 residents) since closing a $5.3B purchase in December 2015; the complex is referenced in the UN Special Rapporteur on the Right to Housing's 22 March 2019 letter to Blackstone's CEO, co-signed by the chair-rapporteur of the UN Working Group on Business and Human Rights, which followed Leilani Farha's 2017 Human Rights Council report on the financialization of housing (A/HRC/34/51). GLOBAL PROPORTION: UN-Habitat's World Cities Report 2026, 'The Global Housing Crisis: Pathways to Action' (launched at WUF13, Baku, May 2026), finds 1.13 billion people living in informal settlements and slums in 2024, up from 895 million in 2000, and approximately 3.4 billion lacking access to secure, safe and adequate housing -- a reminder that NYC's crisis, however severe, is a crisis of price, scarcity and regulation within a fully formal, serviced housing stock, categorically different from the absence of durable shelter facing over a billion people.
global.target: No binding NYC or US target exists for foreign or anonymous capital flows into housing. The relevant global-framework anchor is the UN Special Rapporteur on the Right to Housing's call (since 2017, A/HRC/34/51) for states to ensure housing markets serve human need rather than investment returns. Instruments now in force or in litigation: the NYS pied-a-terre surcharge (enacted 26 May 2026, effective 1 July 2026 -- the first binding NYC-applicable instrument in this space); FinCEN's Residential Real Estate Rule (vacated 19 March 2026, on appeal); the federal Corporate Transparency Act (narrowed March 2025 to foreign-formed entities only); and NY State's LLC Transparency Act (effective 1 Jan 2026, narrowed to non-US-formed LLCs after the 19 Dec 2025 veto of S8432).
global.context: The transmission channel is financial, not physical: global capital reaches NYC housing through shell-company purchases of luxury condos, institutional acquisition of rent-regulated portfolios financed partly through global pension and sovereign capital (as with Ivanhoe Cambridge/CDPQ's stake in Stuyvesant Town), and NYC-headquartered private-equity firms' single-family-rental strategies elsewhere in the US and abroad. This belongs in the Doughnut's global-social lens because it is the mirror image of NYC's local scarcity: the same undersupplied, high-value stock that burdens NYC renters is an attractive store of value for capital raised anywhere. Two honest qualifications. First, the measured magnitude is modest and falling -- 58,810 withheld units is 1.6% of the stock and 43% below 2021 -- so this channel is a real but second-order driver of the 1.41% vacancy rate compared with underproduction. Second, this lens quantifies capital flowing INTO NYC rather than NYC's effect on people elsewhere; it is a transmission-channel reading of R2 rather than an embodied-footprint reading, and no source quantifies the share of NYC purchases made by foreign nationals or anonymous entities. What has changed decisively is visibility: between March 2025 and March 2026 the federal and New York State disclosure regimes were both narrowed to exempt domestic entities and the nationwide residential reporting rule was vacated, leaving the flow less measurable than at any point since 2016 -- at the same moment New York finally enacted a tax on it. A small city like Petaluma has no comparable exposure to global capital markets in its housing stock.
global.source: NYC HPD 2023 NYCHVS (seasonal/occasional-use units); NYS FY2026-27 Budget Bill pied-a-terre provisions as analysed by Holland & Knight; FinCEN news releases, RRE newsroom and Federal Register notices; NY Department of State LLC Transparency Act guidance; OHCHR Special Rapporteur reports and correspondence; UN-Habitat World Cities Report 2026

policyAnchors.name: Housing Stability and Tenant Protection Act (HSTPA) of 2019
policyAnchors.relevance: State law that closed vacancy decontrol and capped preferential-rent and individual/major capital improvement rent increases; NYCHVS confirms that 'legislation enacted in 2019 limited the circumstances under which housing units could exit rent stabilization', underpinning the current 996,600-unit stabilized stock whose size and vacancy dynamics are central to this dossier.
policyAnchors.status: Remains in force; repeatedly cited alongside HVS vacancy math as a reason institutional owners including Blackstone have described profitability pressure on regulated portfolios such as Stuyvesant Town. Not independently re-verified for 2026 amendments in this review pass.

policyAnchors.name: Good Cause Eviction Law (NY State, 2024)
policyAnchors.relevance: Extends just-cause eviction and rent-increase-cap protections to a large share of NYC's previously-unprotected market-rate renters.
policyAnchors.status: In effect since 20 April 2024 in NYC by default; 17 municipalities statewide have since opted in, with approximately 1 million renters covered statewide as of 2025.

policyAnchors.name: 485-x (Affordable Neighborhoods for New Yorkers)
policyAnchors.relevance: Replacement for the expired 421-a tax incentive; ties new-construction tax exemptions to permanent affordability requirements (20-25% of units at a 60-80% AMI weighted average by project tier), permanent rent stabilization of restricted units, construction wage floors and MWBE contracting goals.
policyAnchors.status: Adopted 20 April 2024; construction must commence between 15 June 2022 and 15 June 2034 and complete by 15 June 2038. Existing 421-a(16) projects have an extended completion deadline if they do not convert.

policyAnchors.name: City of Yes for Housing Opportunity
policyAnchors.relevance: Citywide zoning overhaul intended to legalize more housing types (ADUs, small apartment buildings, office conversions) and reduce parking mandates; includes the Universal Affordability Preference (20% density bonus for permanently affordable space) and mandated the Local Law 126 of 2024 basement legalization pilot.
policyAnchors.status: Adopted by City Council 5 December 2024, with a projected 82,000 new homes over 15 years and $5B in accompanying City/State infrastructure funding secured in the Council negotiation. Advocates and researchers argue this falls well short of the scale implied by the 275,000-household growth NYC absorbed between 2021 and 2023 against total housing-stock growth of only 61,000 units.

policyAnchors.name: Fair Housing Framework -- Local Law 167 of 2023 -- and Where We Live NYC
policyAnchors.relevance: Codifies NYC's commitment to affirmatively furthering fair housing; requires HPD and DCP to produce a citywide fair housing assessment and plan every five years, with five-year housing production targets for each community district and a strategic equity framework. Where We Live NYC is the resulting fair-housing plan.
policyAnchors.status: ADJUDICATED IN REVIEW: the Fair Housing Framework is Local Law 167 of 2023 (Int. 1031-2023 / Int. 1031-A), 'A Local Law to amend the New York city charter, in relation to a fair housing plan, and to repeal local law number 133 for the year 2018' -- passed by the Council 15 Nov 2023 and signed by Mayor Adams 13 Dec 2023. The 'LL 174 of 2021' citation that appeared in the research brief is not a real law: the 2021 local laws run 1 through 173, and Local Law 174 of 2017 is the unrelated citywide agency equity-assessment law. 'Where We Live NYC 2025', the city's second five-year fair housing plan, was finalized in 2025.

policyAnchors.name: Right to Counsel (NYC Local Law 136 of 2017; expanded citywide by Local Law 54 of 2021)
policyAnchors.relevance: Guarantees free legal representation to income-eligible tenants facing eviction in Housing Court and NYCHA tenancy-termination proceedings; the single biggest lever shown to keep tenants stably housed (89% remained stably housed with full representation in FY2024).
policyAnchors.status: In effect citywide, but chronically underfunded relative to a full-representation caseload that grew 51% from FY2019 to FY2024 and brief-services demand that grew 475%. Representation fell from 71% (Q4 FY2021) to 42% (Q4 FY2024) and to 30% by March 2025 citywide, and from 81% to 31% in the Bronx, per the NYC Comptroller's May 2025 report. Signed as Int. 214-B on 11 August 2017.

policyAnchors.name: NYCHA PACT/RAD and the Public Housing Preservation Trust
policyAnchors.relevance: Mechanisms for routing private and federal (Section 8/RAD) capital into NYCHA's $78.3B, 20-year physical needs backlog without full privatization.
policyAnchors.status: PACT/RAD conversions continue: 92 developments and 24,639 apartments housing 46,455 authorized residents converted as of the January-2025 Fact Sheet. The Public Housing Preservation Trust (created 2022) provides an additional financing vehicle. The 2023 PNA remains the assessment of record with the next PNA slated for 2028. Not independently re-verified for a mid-2026 status update -- flagged as a data gap.

policyAnchors.name: Local Law 126 of 2024 -- basement and cellar apartment legalization pilot
policyAnchors.relevance: The current legal pathway for the estimated 100,000+ illegally occupied basement and cellar units citywide, mandated by City of Yes for Housing Opportunity; the direct policy response to the 11 basement drowning deaths in Hurricane Ida.
policyAnchors.status: DOB and HPD published proposed rules in November 2025. Eligibility is limited to apartments that existed before 20 April 2024, in community districts named in the law, with basic safety features (smoke and gas alarms, central heating, adequate egress, boiler separation). Owners have until 20 April 2029 to apply and 10 years to reach full compliance. Properties in flood-prone areas are categorically ineligible -- excluding the exposure that caused the 2021 deaths. Its predecessor, the 2019 BACPP pilot in Brooklyn CD5, completed zero conversions.

policyAnchors.name: NYC Rent Guidelines Board 2026-27 rent freeze
policyAnchors.relevance: First-ever freeze applied to both 1-year and 2-year rent-stabilized lease renewals; a direct, near-term test of Mayor Mamdani's affordability agenda given the RGB's role as sole regulator of rents on 996,600 units.
policyAnchors.status: Approved 7-1 by the RGB on 25 June 2026; 0% increase for both lease lengths effective 1 Oct 2026 to 30 Sept 2027. A pro-landlord board member resigned in protest hours before the vote. Landlord groups and some housing economists argue the freeze does not address underlying vacancy/supply scarcity and could reduce maintenance investment; tenant advocates frame it as immediate relief for burdened renters.

policyAnchors.name: NYS pied-a-terre surcharge (FY2026-27 Budget Bill)
policyAnchors.relevance: The first binding fiscal instrument aimed at non-primary-residence ownership of NYC housing, after roughly seven years of failed proposals; directly addresses the global-lens channel of housing held as a store of value rather than a home.
policyAnchors.status: Enacted 26 May 2026 as part of the NYS FY2026-27 Budget Bill; effective 1 July 2026 with a component retroactive to 1 January 2026; sunsets 30 June 2031 unless extended. Phase 1 (to 30 June 2028): Class 2 condos and co-ops above $1M taxed at 4.0% / 5.25% / 6.5% by bracket; Class 1 homes above $5M at 0.8% / 1.05% / 1.3%. Phase 2 (2028-2031) applies a $5M threshold across all classes. An estimated ~14,000 NYC units are in scope; the Comptroller has revised expected revenue to $340-380M from an initial $500M.

social.comparisonNote: Petaluma's housing entry (data.js, level 60) reports 34% cost-burdened households and 214 unhoused persons (point-in-time count, 2024) against a target of <30% burdened and zero unhoused -- serious for a city of ~60,000, but a single-order-of-magnitude problem measured with a straightforward annual PIT count. NYC's housing crisis is legally structural rather than simply a burden rate: a 1.41% vacancy rate is itself the statutory trigger sustaining rent stabilization for 996,600 units. NYC is also worse on the burden metric, not merely bigger -- just over half of NYC renter households are rent-burdened on the ACS basis against Petaluma's 34%, with 28.9% severely burdened -- and at 8.3M people the affected population is roughly two orders of magnitude larger. NYC's shelter system alone served 194,531 unique people in 2025, roughly 900x Petaluma's entire PIT unhoused count and about 2.3% of NYC's population passing through DHS shelter in a single year, with more than 350,000 New Yorkers without homes at the start of 2026. NYC also carries two housing dimensions Petaluma has no equivalent of: a $78.3B public-housing capital backlog (NYCHA, 511,384 residents) and a global-capital dynamic -- anonymous-LLC and non-primary-residence ownership, private-equity ownership of regulated stock -- that a small inland city simply is not exposed to. The one respect in which NYC is moving faster than Petaluma is policy: City of Yes, Good Cause Eviction, 485-x, a rent freeze and an enacted pied-a-terre tax all landed within 26 months.

social.name: peace & justice
social.levelRationale: Anchored on the headline homicide rate, this dimension would score deep in safe territory alone (roughly -80): 305 murders in 2025, down 20.2% from 382 in 2024, a rate of ~3.6/100,000 — among the lowest in NYC's modern recorded history and well below the national average. But R1 requires adjusting for well-sourced shortfalls captured in the same dimension, and here they are severe, not marginal. PULLING THE LEVEL UP: (1) a federal court held the city in CONTEMPT in Nov 2024 for ongoing constitutional violations at Rikers (use-of-force, staff accountability, supervision failures); (2) the court then ordered a Remediation Manager with powers equivalent to a receiver (May 2025 order; powers detailed Dec 19, 2025; Nicholas Deml named Jan 2026) — the city has lost operational control of a core agency, an outcome with no precedent in the Nunez litigation's history; (3) in-custody deaths rebounded to 15 in 2025 from a low of 5 in 2024 (Vera Institute tracking), still below 2022's 19 but a reversal; (4) the average daily jail population (~6,747, Jan-May 2026) runs roughly 1.6-2x the 3,300-4,160 capacity the closure plan requires, and the city's own Mamdani administration has now formally acknowledged the Aug 31, 2027 legal deadline to close Rikers will be missed, with replacement jails not complete until 2029-2032; (5) 12+ years after the Floyd remedial order, NYPD accountability remains structurally weak: CCRB complaints hit a decade-high in 2024 (5,663), NYPD implements fewer than half of CCRB's substantiated non-disciplinary recommendations, and the city paid $117M-$206M/year in misconduct settlements (2024-2025); (6) stop-and-frisk racial disparities persist even as volume fell — Black drivers were 32% of NYPD's 2M+ 2024 traffic stops against ~20-23% of the city's population, and searched at roughly 9x the rate of white drivers. Net: street-level violence is a genuine, well-evidenced NYC strength; the carceral and police-accountability side of this dimension is a genuine, court-documented crisis. The two do not average to a mild score — they coexist, and the level (45, 'needs attention' tilting toward critical) is deliberately anchored closer to the carceral-system failure because it represents an active, unresolved federal constitutional violation, which this framework treats as more structurally severe than a favorable-but-improving crime trend.

Note press variance in early tallies (302-303-309 reported before final NYPD compilation) — 305 is the figure in the joint NYPD/Governor's Office year-end release and is treated as authoritative per R11.

NYC recorded its lowest murder total in the modern CompStat era in 2025, a genuine and heavily-verified result (multiple independent city, state, and press sources converge on ~305, -20%). This is the headline strength of the dimension. But 'peace & justice' in the Doughnut framework is not only about violence between residents — it is also about the justice system's treatment of the people it holds, and there NYC's headline number tells a starkly different story: a federal judge found the city in contempt of a 13-year-old consent judgment, then took the unprecedented step of ordering a court-appointed Remediation Manager (functionally a receiver) with hiring/firing and policy-making authority over DOC, because in-custody deaths and use-of-force incidents kept rising despite four mayoral administrations' worth of monitoring. NYC is simultaneously one of the safest large US cities on the street and running a jail system a federal court has found unconstitutional — a genuine structural tension, not a data error, and the two facts must be reported side by side rather than blended into a false middle. The policy lever for the carceral crisis is the Nunez remediation process and the borough-based jails construction timeline; the lever for street violence is continued precision-policing and Crisis Management System investment, which itself faces funding pressure (see subIndicators).

global.levelRationale: Two real, quantified transmission channels exist for this dimension, pulling in opposite directions, and neither has an established benchmark or fair-share target to score severity against — so per R2, this is scored null with strong framing rather than forced into a number. (1) NYC as a destination for people fleeing conflict and persecution: more than 237,000 asylum seekers have come through the city's care since spring 2022 (city-scale, quantified, a genuine positive contribution to global displacement response, tracked against a 117.8M-person global forcibly-displaced population at end of 2025 per UNHCR). (2) NYC's financial sector as a capital allocator to the industries this dimension is concerned with: NYC's public pension funds' Palantir holdings — a firm with major ICE and defense/surveillance contracts — grew from ~$17.6M (2022) to ~$56.6M (2024), and the funds hold $1.5M+ in Elbit Systems (an Israeli arms manufacturer) as part of ~$300M in Israeli-company equities, per December 2025 disclosures. There is no accepted way to net a refugee-hosting figure against a portfolio-holdings figure into one severity score, and no external target defines how much of either NYC 'should' have. Both figures are carried here, quantified and sourced, rather than compressed into an invented level.

social.levelRationale: Anchored on the published headline: 20.6% of NYC workers drove alone to work (ACS 2024 1-Year, place-level), against the shared <50% threshold used in the Petaluma portrait. At 41% of the threshold this argues for roughly -85 on the headline alone. Moved up ~20 points under R1 for two material, independently verified structural failures inside the same dimension: (1) SUBWAY ACCESSIBILITY -- only 160 of 472 stations (33.9%) have stair-free access per MTA's own July 2026 count, leaving ~66% inaccessible, with the court-approved compliance horizon set at 2055; (2) BUS SPEEDS -- 8.17 mph citywide in 2024, DOWN 0.6% from 8.22 mph in 2015 and far short of the City's own 25%-improvement goal, with Manhattan at 6.29 mph. Also pulling up, though less: mean commute time of 40.6 minutes, among the longest of any large US city; Staten Island at 50.8% is the one borough above the threshold; Fair Fares enrolls only 41% of its ~940,000 eligible population; and NYC DOT has missed its Local Law 195 bus- and bike-lane mileage mandates every recent year. NOT moved further up, for three reasons independently verified in adversarial review: (a) TRAFFIC SAFETY IS A STRENGTH, NOT A SHORTFALL -- 2025 recorded 205 traffic deaths, the fewest since record-keeping began in 1910, down 19% year-on-year and 31% since Vision Zero launched in 2014, with Q1 2026 the third-lowest on record; an earlier version of this rationale asserted fatalities were at post-Vision-Zero highs, which primary NYC DOT sources refute; (b) the Fair Fares gap is smaller than previously stated (41% of ~940,000, not 37% of 1.4M) and is closing, with the income ceiling raised to 150% FPL and a further expansion to 200% FPL agreed in June 2026; (c) congestion pricing is operating, legally secure following Judge Liman's final ruling of 3 March 2026 in Metropolitan Transportation Authority v. Duffy, and delivering measured reductions (11% fewer vehicle entries, 27 million fewer entries in year one). Per R5, a strongly negative level is the correct and honest result for NYC mobility mode share and has not been nudged toward zero.

Brooklyn: 17.0% drove alone (211,612 of 1,247,694 workers 16+); mean travel time to work 41.7 min (+-0.5)

Citywide for comparison: 20.6% citywide (840,263 of 4,070,607 workers 16+) drove alone in 2024 -- the officially published figure for the Census place 'New York city, New York'. Full published mode share: 48.7% public transportation, 12.5% worked from home, 9.6% walked, 4.4% carpooled, 1.7% bicycle, 1.2% other, 1.1% taxicab, 0.2% motorcycle. Only 25.1% of workers used a car, truck or van at all. DENOMINATOR NOTE: the ACS universe for this table is all workers 16+ INCLUDING those who worked from home, which is the same basis as Petaluma's 72.6% and therefore the correct comparison. If the work-from-home population is excluded from the denominator (i.e. mode share among people who actually travel to work), drove-alone rises to 23.6% (840,263 of 3,560,755). Both figures are stated because the 12.5% work-from-home share materially affects the percentage. By borough, drove-alone ranges from 5.2% in Manhattan to 50.8% in Staten Island -- a ~46-point spread within one city.

This is the dimension where NYC and Petaluma diverge most sharply: Petaluma's 72.6% drive-alone rate vs. NYC's 20.6% reflects two fundamentally different built environments -- a car-dependent small city vs. a transit-first megacity with the country's only 24/7 subway system. But a low drive-alone rate does not mean NYC's mobility system is healthy. Two failures are severe and well-evidenced: only about a third of subway stations (160 of 472) offer stair-free access, with the court-approved compliance horizon at 2055; and bus speeds have not improved in a decade, running at 8.17 mph citywide and 6.29 mph in Manhattan against the City's own goal of a 25% improvement. Mean commute time, 40.6 minutes, is among the longest of any large US city. Traffic safety, by contrast, is now a genuine strength: 2025 was the safest year in recorded NYC history (205 deaths, down 31% since Vision Zero began in 2014), and the first quarter of 2026 was the third-safest on record. The policy lever with the most momentum is congestion pricing (Central Business District Tolling Program), which is reshaping the denominator itself by pulling trips out of cars, and which survived the federal attempt to terminate it with a final court ruling in the MTA's favour in March 2026. NOTE on a claim removed in review: the widely-repeated assertion that NYC buses are 'the slowest of any major US city' is not supported by the NYC Comptroller report usually cited for it and could not be sourced to a primary comparative dataset, so it is not asserted here; what the source does support is a decade of stagnation against the City's own target.
social.source: US Census Bureau ACS 2024 1-Year, Tables B08301 and S0801, Kings County, New York
actions: Apply for Fair Fares NYC through ACCESS HRA if household income is at or below 150% of the Federal Poverty Level (rising to 200% FPL in fall 2026) and you are aged 18-64 -- only about 41% of the ~940,000 currently eligible New Yorkers are enrolled (nyc.gov/site/hra/help/fair-fares.page).

Submit testimony or comment to NYC DOT / City Council on Streets Plan (LL195) compliance, since the agency has missed its statutory annual bus- and bike-lane mileage mandates every recent year measured.

Track and comment on the Interborough Express (IBX) scoping and environmental review through MTA's project page as it moves toward a Draft Environmental Impact Statement (mta.info/project/interborough-express).

Support or monitor the MTA subway accessibility capital program (2025-2029, $7.1B) -- the Center for Independence of the Disabled, New York, lead plaintiff in the settlement, tracks compliance with the interim milestones; 160 of 472 stations are accessible today against a 2055 deadline.

Press for faster bus service through the MTA/DOT bus priority programme (busways, camera-enforced bus lanes, all-door boarding), since citywide bus speeds have not improved in a decade (8.17 mph in 2024 vs 8.22 in 2015) against the City's own 25%-improvement goal.
Use and provide feedback on Vision Zero infrastructure (20 mph zones under Sammy's Law, open streets, protected bike and bus lanes) via NYC DOT's public engagement channels (nyc.gov/visionzero).

Follow congestion pricing's toll-schedule developments (rising to $12 in 2028 and $15 in 2031) via MTA's Congestion Relief Zone page, and check eligibility for the Low-Income Discount Plan, which halves the peak toll from the 11th trip in a calendar month.

reviewStatus.notes: Corrections from an independent adversarial review applied.

social.boroughsNote: The five borough worker totals sum to exactly 4,070,607 and the five borough drove-alone counts to exactly 840,263 -- identical to the published place-level totals for New York city, New York. No borough figure is interpolated, pro-rated or derived; all five are published county estimates.
social.neighborhoodNote: Bay Terrace, Fresh Meadows, Glen Oaks and Oakland Gardens in northeastern/eastern Queens are documented transit deserts: no subway access, with residents dependent on express buses and the LIRR. A Streetsblog NYC op-ed (January 2020) on the Queens bus-network redesign named these neighborhoods specifically, noting the redesign would cut them from all-day, seven-day express bus service to weekday rush hours only, even though their lack of transit alternatives is what makes the express bus a lifeline. This contrasts with Manhattan's near-universal subway proximity (5.2% drive-alone, 51.0% transit). CAVEATS ADDED IN REVIEW: an earlier version attributed these neighborhoods to 'roughly Community District 11' -- they in fact span several different Queens community districts, so no single CD is named here. An earlier version also claimed 'fewer than 4 in 10 Queens residents overall can walk to a subway station'; that statistic could not be sourced and has been removed. The nearest sourceable figure is a citywide one (more than a third of all New Yorkers do not live within walking distance of a subway or rail station), which is a different measure at a different geography. A Queens-specific subway-walkshed percentage remains a dataGap.

subIndicators.name: Subway stations with ADA (stair-free) accessibility
subIndicators.value: 160 of 472 subway stations accessible (33.9%) as of July 2026 -- meaning roughly 66% of stations remain stair-inaccessible. MTA states this is 'nearly eleven times the 15 stations that were accessible when the ADA passed in 1990'. The Governor's office reported 154 accessible as of 31 December 2025 after 10 station accessibility projects completed during 2025, consistent with 160 by mid-2026. The 2022/2023 class-action settlement baseline was 364 inaccessible stations of 472, i.e. 108 accessible (~23%) at time of settlement.
subIndicators.source: MTA (primary), accessibility article updated 22 July 2026; MTA ADA Settlement Notice for the 2023 baseline; NY Governor's Office 31 December 2025 release for the 154 interim count
subIndicators.reviewNote: Upgraded from secondary reporting (HelpNewYork.com / amNewYork) to an MTA primary statement during adversarial review.

subIndicators.name: MTA subway/SIR accessibility settlement commitment
subIndicators.value: Settlement commits the MTA to making at least 95% of the 364 stations that were inaccessible at the time of settlement stair-free accessible by 2055 (equivalently ~454 of 472 stations, ~96% systemwide), via interim milestones: 81 stations already contracted in the 2020-2024 or prior capital plans, then +85 by 2035, +90 by 2045, +90 by 2055 (81+85+90+90 = 346 = 95% of 364). The MTA must dedicate no less than 14.69% of the NYC Transit portion of any capital plan of $35.389B or more to station accessibility, with a floor of 8%. Consolidated cases: Center for Independence of the Disabled, New York, et al. v. MTA (NY State Supreme Court, No. 153765/2017) and De La Rosa, et al. v. MTA (S.D.N.Y., No. 19-cv-04406); fairness hearings scheduled April 2023.
subIndicators.source: MTA ADA Settlement Notice (primary)
subIndicators.reviewNote: Corrected in review: the 95% target applies to the 364 then-inaccessible stations, not to all 472 as previously stated. The milestone arithmetic (346 = 95% of 364) confirms the corrected base.

subIndicators.name: Mean travel time to work
subIndicators.value: 40.6 minutes (+-0.3) citywide -- among the longest of any large US city. By borough: Manhattan 31.4, Brooklyn 41.7, Bronx 43.3, Queens 43.8, Staten Island 45.4.
subIndicators.source: US Census Bureau, ACS 2024 1-Year Estimates, Subject Table S0801 (variable S0801_C01_046), place 'New York city, New York' -- officially published at city level
subIndicators.reviewNote: Replaced an author-derived worker-weighted estimate of ~40.4 minutes with the published place-level figure of 40.6, per R3. Manhattan corrected from 31.5 (+-0.4) to the published 31.4 (+-0.6).

subIndicators.name: Super-commuters (90+ minute one-way commute)
subIndicators.value: Staten Island (Richmond County) reported as having the 5th-highest super-commuter share of any US county at 14.3%; elevated super-commuting documented across the outer boroughs and concentrated among public-transit riders (14.0% of transit commuters vs. 2.4% of drivers).
subIndicators.source: Apartment List / Stacker analysis of Census commuting microdata (secondary; not independently re-verified against a primary Census tabulation in this review)
subIndicators.reviewNote: Confidence lowered to low: this rests on a third-party analysis that was not re-fetched or confirmed against a primary Census table during adversarial review.

subIndicators.name: Average bus speed
subIndicators.value: 8.17 mph citywide in 2024 -- DOWN 0.6% from 8.22 mph in 2015 (8.06 in 2019), i.e. a decade of no improvement, and far short of the City's stated goal of improving bus speeds citywide by 25%. By borough (2024): Staten Island 12.6 mph, Queens 8.75, Bronx 7.65, Brooklyn 7.37, Manhattan 6.29 (slowest). Manhattan is the only borough faster in 2024 than in 2015 (+3%); Staten Island slowed most (-8%). The M42 crosstown is the single slowest route citywide at 5.27 mph (2025), and eight of the city's ten slowest routes are inside the congestion relief zone. Buses also fail to reach stops on schedule 30% of the time (37% for express buses).
subIndicators.source: NYC Comptroller, Bureau of Policy and Research, "Behind Schedule: How New York City's Bus System Slow Rolls Riders", April 2025 (Table 3 and Table 8), drawing on MTA bus speed data
subIndicators.reviewNote: All borough and citywide speeds confirmed digit-for-digit against Table 3 of the primary PDF. M42 corrected from 5.25 to 5.27 mph. The claim that NYC buses are 'the slowest of any major US city' was REMOVED: it appears nowhere in the cited report and could not be sourced to a primary comparative dataset.

subIndicators.name: Vision Zero traffic fatalities
subIndicators.value: 205 traffic deaths in 2025 -- the fewest ever recorded, dating back to when NYC record-keeping began in 1910, and one fewer than the previous record year (206 in 2018). Down 19% from 253 in 2024 and down 31% since Vision Zero launched in 2014. Pedestrian deaths 111 in 2025 vs. 122 in 2024 (-9%); child fatalities 6 vs. 16 (-63%); total injuries down 7.7% (47,557 vs 51,540) and serious injuries down 2.8% (2,947 vs 3,031). The improvement has continued: 42 deaths in the first three months of 2026, down 7% year-on-year and the third-fewest recorded at that point in the year since 1910 (only 2015 and 2018 were lower).
subIndicators.source: NYC DOT press releases, "Traffic Deaths Reach All-time Low" (January 2026) and "Traffic Deaths Are Near Lowest Levels in Recorded History After First Three Months of 2026"
subIndicators.reviewNote: MATERIAL CORRECTION FROM REVIEW. An earlier framing described recent years as 'among the deadliest of the Vision Zero era' and the dimension's level rationale treated traffic fatalities as a factor pushing severity upward. Primary NYC DOT sources refute that framing for the current period: 2025 is the safest year in recorded NYC history and Q1 2026 is the third-safest on record. Traffic safety is a verified STRENGTH of this dimension, not a shortfall, and is scored as such.

subIndicators.name: Fair Fares NYC enrollment vs. eligibility
subIndicators.value: About 385,000 of the 938,834 (~940,000) income-eligible New Yorkers are enrolled in the half-price transit fare program -- 41% of eligible, leaving 59% of eligible New Yorkers unenrolled. Eligibility is currently 150% of the Federal Poverty Level ($23,940 for a single adult, $49,500 for a household of four) for residents aged 18-64; adults 65+ and many disabled New Yorkers are excluded because they qualify for the MTA's separate Reduced-Fare program, and the Fair Fares discount does not apply to express buses. The threshold has risen from below 100% FPL at 2019 launch to 120% (2023) to 145% (2025) to 150%; in June 2026 the City Council and Mayor agreed to raise it to 200% FPL effective fall 2026, adding an estimated 342,604 newly eligible New Yorkers (total eligible rising to ~1.28 million). Earlier figure for trend: ~360,000 enrolled at end-2024 = 38% of eligible.
subIndicators.source: NYC Independent Budget Office, "Expanding Fair Fares: Many Options, A Range of Costs" (June 2026), based on IBO analysis of HRA enrollment data and ACS 2024 1-Year estimates; NYC Comptroller "Behind Schedule" (April 2025) for the end-2024 figure; NY1 (30 June 2026) for the 200% FPL agreement
subIndicators.reviewNote: CORRECTED IN REVIEW. The previous value ('~37% of the ~1.4 million income-eligible') was wrong on both numbers and internally impossible -- it implied ~518,000 enrollees, which no primary source supports. The 1.4 million figure is the eligible pool AFTER the future 200% FPL expansion, not the current one. The previous policy status ('145% FPL, with a further increase to 150% underway') was also stale: 150% is already in effect and 200% was agreed in June 2026. The under-enrollment shortfall is real but milder than previously stated and is closing.

subIndicators.name: NYC Streets Plan (LL195) mileage shortfall
subIndicators.value: DOT built 18.2 lane-miles of protected bike lanes in 2025 (36% of the 50-mile/year statutory minimum) and 13.5 lane-miles of protected bus lanes in 2024 (45% of the 30-mile/year minimum). 2024's ~29 bike-lane miles was reportedly the third-highest annual total in city history, yet still fell short of the legal mandate in every year checked.
subIndicators.source: City & State New York, "NYC DOT falls far short of '24 targets for bike and bus lanes" (secondary; not independently re-verified against a primary DOT compliance filing in this review)
subIndicators.reviewNote: Not re-fetched in this review pass; confidence set to medium pending confirmation against NYC DOT's own Local Law 195 annual compliance reporting.

subIndicators.name: Congestion pricing (Central Business District Tolling Program / Congestion Relief Zone)
subIndicators.value: Launched 5 January 2025 at 12:00 AM. Current toll for Class 1 passenger vehicles with E-ZPass: $9.00 peak (5am-9pm weekdays, 9am-9pm weekends) and $2.25 overnight, per the TBTA tariff, which sets Phase 1 at 2025-2027 ($9.00/$2.25), Phase 2 at 2028-2030 ($12.00/$3.00) and Phase 3 from 2031 ($15.00/$3.75). A registered Low-Income Discount Plan halves the peak toll from the 11th trip in a calendar month. First-year measured effects (through ~November 2025): ~27 million fewer vehicle entries into the zone (11% average daily decline, ~73,000 fewer vehicles/day); vehicle miles travelled down 7.1%; morning-rush travel-time gains at major crossings (Holland Tunnel 51% faster, Queensboro Bridge 29.3%, Lincoln Tunnel 24.7%, Brooklyn Bridge 15%, Manhattan Bridge 6.7%); in-zone weekday vehicle speeds up 4%, weekend 6.2%, bus speeds 2.3%, truck speeds 5.6%; subway trips into the zone up 9%, express bus up 7.8%, local bus up 8.4%; $518M net toll revenue through November 2025 against a $500M/yr target, projected to exceed $550M. LITIGATION RESOLVED IN THE CITY'S FAVOUR: in Metropolitan Transportation Authority v. Duffy (S.D.N.Y., filed 19 February 2025), Judge Lewis Liman granted the MTA a preliminary injunction in May 2025 and then, on 3 March 2026, issued a final 149-page decision holding that the federal administration lacked authority to terminate the program and that its attempted revocation of approval was arbitrary and capricious. Four other federal challenges (Chan, Mulgrew, New Yorkers Against Congestion Pricing Tax, Trucking Association) were closed on summary judgment for defendants on 17 April 2025. No court has ordered the program to halt, and it is operating.
subIndicators.source: MTA/TBTA CBD toll tariff (primary, for toll amounts and phase years); Governor Hochul first-anniversary release and MTA press releases (for measured first-year outcomes); Regional Plan Association congestion pricing litigation tracker and reporting on the 3 March 2026 ruling (for litigation status)
subIndicators.reviewNote: Toll amounts and phase years verified against the MTA primary tariff document. Litigation status updated in review: the previous entry stopped at the May 2025 preliminary injunction and missed the 3 March 2026 final ruling, which is the materially more significant outcome. A secondary claim circulating that congestion pricing is 'suspended by executive action' in 2026 was checked and is false.
subIndicators.geographicScaleNote: city (Manhattan CBD zone, with regional spillover effects)

subIndicators.name: Interborough Express (IBX)
subIndicators.value: Proposed 14-mile light-rail line connecting Brooklyn and Queens along an existing freight right-of-way, bypassing Manhattan; projected 160,000+ daily riders. As of 2026 the project is in design/environmental review; MTA estimates it would eliminate 21.8 million vehicle-miles of car trips annually once built. No construction start date confirmed.
subIndicators.source: MTA press release, Earth Day 2026 IBX vehicle-miles announcement; MTA project page (not independently re-verified in this review pass)
subIndicators.reviewNote: Not re-fetched in this review pass; confidence set to medium.

subIndicators.name: Sammy's Law / 20 mph speed limits
subIndicators.value: State legislation (Sammy's Law, 2024) authorized NYC for the first time to lower default speed limits without separate state approval. NYC DOT began lowering limits from 25 to 20 mph in 2024 and reported completing rollout across 250 designated zones/areas by the end of 2025.
subIndicators.source: News aggregation of NYC DOT rollout reporting (secondary; not independently re-verified against a primary NYC DOT or NY State source in this review pass)
subIndicators.reviewNote: Confidence lowered to low: the only cited source is a news aggregator. A primary NYC DOT or NY State legislative citation is needed.

global.levelRationale: Scored null per ruling R2. The only quantified material available for this lens is a comparative construction-cost benchmark, which R2 explicitly rules out as a headline global indicator: 'NYC's subway construction costs are the highest in the world' is a governance and cost-efficiency fact about NYC, not a claim about NYC's effect on anyone beyond its boundary. That figure is retained below as a subIndicator. The genuinely global-facing threads -- NYC's transferability as the one large US city whose mode share is compatible with a 1.5C-aligned per-capita transport budget, the supply chains embodied in its rolling stock and electric bus fleet, and the aviation emissions of JFK/LaGuardia/Newark that sit outside the city's GPC inventory boundary -- are all real but none is quantified for NYC in this research pass. Per R2, an honest qualitative framing with a null level and named parties who could quantify it is the correct output; attaching a precise-looking score (the previous entry carried level 30 on no underlying quantity) would be a finding, not a result.
global.indicator: NYC's external mobility footprint and its transferability as a low-car megacity model -- qualitative pending quantification of (a) rolling-stock and electric-bus supply-chain sourcing, (b) aviation emissions excluded from the city inventory boundary, and (c) the transport-mode-share transferability argument
global.value: NOT QUANTIFIED. Three transmission channels are identified but none has a defensible NYC-specific number in this pass. (1) TRANSFERABILITY: NYC is the one large US city where a large majority of workers do not use a car to get to work (25.1% used a car, truck or van at all; 48.7% used public transit; 9.6% walked), which is the empirical basis on which dense transit-oriented development is argued globally to be compatible with a 1.5C per-capita transport budget. Quantifying NYC's per-capita transport emissions against a downscaled global transport budget would turn this into a real global indicator; that calculation has not been done here. (2) SUPPLY CHAIN: the embodied emissions and labour conditions in MTA rolling-stock procurement and electric-bus/battery sourcing are a genuine external footprint, but no NYC-specific quantification was located and this channel was not researched in this pass. (3) AVIATION: JFK, LaGuardia and Newark aviation emissions are widely reported to fall outside NYC's official GPC-protocol greenhouse-gas inventory boundary, which would make a substantial share of the mobility emissions NYC induces invisible in its own accounting. The primary source for this (Citizens Budget Commission) returned HTTP 403 on two separate fetch attempts, including during adversarial review, and the claim is therefore NOT asserted -- it remains a dataGap for MOCEJ and the Port Authority of NY & NJ to resolve. GLOBAL-EQUITY COUNTERPOINT (context, not an NYC-attributable metric): roughly 900 million to 1 billion rural people worldwide lack access to an all-season road (World Bank Rural Access Index / SDG indicator 9.1.1), a stark contrast with NYC's 24/7 rail system, but not something NYC policy moves.
global.target: No quantified target can be scored against until one of the three channels above is quantified. If NYC's per-capita transport emissions were computed, the appropriate benchmark would be a downscaled 1.5C-aligned per-capita transport budget applied identically across all portraits in the repo, consistent with rulings R8 and R12.
global.context: NYC's below-25%-car mode share is precisely the outcome climate and transit advocates worldwide point to as proof that dense transit-oriented cities work, and the city exports that model through comparative research and city networks (Transit Costs Project, ITDP, C40). The cost subIndicator below is the cautionary half of that story -- at $4B+ per mile NYC cannot build enough subway to close its own accessibility gaps -- but per R2 it describes NYC's governance, not NYC's effect on others, and so cannot carry this lens. The honest position is that mobility's global lens is currently unquantified, and that the fastest route to quantifying it is either the aviation-boundary question (MOCEJ / Port Authority) or a rolling-stock procurement footprint (MTA Construction & Development).
global.source: See subIndicators and dataGaps; no single source carries this lens.
global.productionVsConsumptionNote: not applicable as structured; the aviation-emissions boundary question is inherently a production-based-inventory-scope issue and could not be verified this pass

policyAnchors.name: Central Business District Tolling Program / Congestion Relief Zone (congestion pricing)
policyAnchors.relevance: Primary near-term lever changing NYC's mobility mode share and traffic volumes; direct funding source for the MTA capital accessibility program.
policyAnchors.status: Live and operating since 5 January 2025. Current Class 1 E-ZPass toll $9.00 peak / $2.25 overnight (tariff Phase 1, 2025-2027; $12.00 in Phase 2, 2028-2030; $15.00 from 2031). The federal attempt to terminate the program has FAILED on the merits: Judge Lewis Liman, S.D.N.Y., granted the MTA a preliminary injunction in May 2025 and issued a final 149-page ruling on 3 March 2026 in Metropolitan Transportation Authority v. Duffy holding that the administration lacked authority to terminate and that the revocation was arbitrary and capricious. First-year outcomes (traffic down ~11%, VMT down 7.1%, faster crossings, $518M net revenue through November 2025) published by MTA and the Governor's office.

policyAnchors.name: NYC Streets Plan (Local Law 195 of 2019)
policyAnchors.relevance: Statutory minimum annual mileage for protected bus lanes (30 mi/yr) and protected bike lanes (50 mi/yr); the core accountability mechanism for street redesign.
policyAnchors.status: In effect but DOT has missed the mandate every recent year measured (2025: 18.2 mi bike lanes = 36% of mandate; 2024: 13.5 mi bus lanes = 45% of mandate). City Council was considering added tracking and oversight legislation as of April 2025. These figures rest on secondary reporting and should be confirmed against DOT's own LL195 compliance filings.

policyAnchors.name: MTA subway accessibility class-action settlement
policyAnchors.relevance: Binding, court-approved commitment on the pace of subway ADA accessibility upgrades -- the lever on the local-social lens's largest documented failure.
policyAnchors.status: Settlement in Center for Independence of the Disabled, New York v. MTA (NY State, 153765/2017) and De La Rosa v. MTA (S.D.N.Y., 19-cv-04406); fairness hearings April 2023. Commits the MTA to stair-free access at 95% of the 364 stations inaccessible at settlement by 2055, with interim milestones of +85 by 2035, +90 by 2045 and +90 by 2055 on top of 81 already contracted. 160 of 472 stations (33.9%) accessible as of July 2026, up from 108 at settlement and 154 at end-2025. The 2025-2029 Capital Program dedicates $7.1B to accessibility, targeting 60+ newly accessible stations this cycle.

policyAnchors.name: Sammy's Law (NY State, 2024)
policyAnchors.relevance: State authorization enabling NYC to set 20 mph default speed limits without prior state sign-off; directly supports Vision Zero.
policyAnchors.status: Reported as implemented, with DOT completing rollout of 20 mph limits across 250 designated zones by end of 2025. Sourced only to news aggregation in this pass -- needs a primary NYC DOT or NY State citation.

policyAnchors.name: Vision Zero (2014)
policyAnchors.relevance: The city's overarching traffic-safety policy framework; sets the baseline against which the record-low fatality counts are measured.
policyAnchors.status: Active and delivering. 2025 was the safest year in recorded NYC history (205 deaths, the fewest since record-keeping began in 1910, down 31% since the 2014 launch and one below the prior record of 206 in 2018). The first quarter of 2026 was the third-safest on record (42 deaths, down 7% year-on-year). This corrects an earlier characterization of recent years as among the era's deadliest.

policyAnchors.name: Fair Fares NYC
policyAnchors.relevance: City's primary transit-affordability program for low-income residents; the enrollment gap is a direct equity lever within the mobility dimension.
policyAnchors.status: Eligibility currently 150% FPL for residents aged 18-64; ~385,000 of ~940,000 eligible enrolled (41%). In June 2026 the City Council and Mayor agreed to raise the threshold to 200% FPL effective fall 2026, adding ~343,000 newly eligible (total eligible ~1.28M). The discount still does not apply to express buses, and adults 65+ and many disabled New Yorkers remain excluded because they qualify for the MTA's separate Reduced-Fare program.

social.comparisonNote: Petaluma's 72.6% drive-alone commute share (a small Mediterranean-climate city built almost entirely around cars) sits at nearly the opposite end of the spectrum from NYC's published 20.6% citywide figure -- and even NYC's most car-dependent borough, Staten Island, at 50.8%, is still well below Petaluma's rate. Both figures are ACS drive-alone shares of all workers 16+, including those who work from home, so they are directly comparable (R4). But the comparison cuts both ways: Petaluma has no subway to fail at accessibility, no multi-billion-dollar-per-mile construction-cost problem, and no decade-long traffic-safety programme comparable to Vision Zero. NYC's real failures here -- two-thirds of subway stations without stair-free access on a 2055 timetable, buses averaging 8.17 mph with no improvement in ten years, and 40.6-minute average commutes -- are failures of scale and complexity that a 60,000-person city never has to confront. Equally, NYC's traffic-safety record (fewest deaths since 1910) and its working congestion charge are achievements for which Petaluma has no equivalent lever.
dataGaps: Borough-by-borough count of ADA-accessible subway stations. MTA publishes a citywide total (160 of 472 as of July 2026) and a station-by-station list, but not a per-borough total or denominator, so per-borough accessibility percentages cannot be computed. MTA Department of Subways / Accessibility unit holds this.

A Queens-specific figure for the share of residents within walking distance of a subway station. The claim 'fewer than 4 in 10 Queens residents can walk to a subway station' could not be sourced and has been removed; only a citywide figure (more than a third of New Yorkers not within walking distance of a subway or rail station) was locatable. NYC Department of City Planning or the MTA could produce a borough-level subway walkshed statistic.

Whether JFK/LaGuardia/Newark aviation emissions are formally excluded from MOCEJ's citywide GHG inventory boundary, and by how much. The Mayor's Office of Climate & Environmental Justice (MOCEJ) or the Port Authority of NY & NJ holds the definitive inventory-boundary documentation; the secondary source (Citizens Budget Commission) returned HTTP 403 on repeated fetch attempts and could not be verified. This is the single highest-value gap for the global lens.

A quantified embodied-emissions or supply-chain footprint for MTA rolling stock and electric bus/battery procurement, which would give the global-social lens a real number in place of its current null. MTA Construction & Development and the MTA procurement office hold the contract and sourcing data.
NYC DOT's own Local Law 195 compliance filings, to replace the secondary reporting currently carrying the Streets Plan mileage-shortfall figures.
A primary NYC DOT or NY State citation for the Sammy's Law 20 mph rollout, currently sourced only to a news aggregator.

A primary comparative dataset (e.g. National Transit Database) on average bus speed across large US transit agencies, which would either substantiate or retire the widely-repeated claim that NYC buses are the slowest of any major US city.

ecological.name: climate change
ecological.levelRationale: Scored under ruling R12 against the DEAL 1.5C-aligned per-capita benchmark (1.6-2.0 tCO2e/person), NOT against NYC's own 40x30 statutory target. NYC's production-based emissions are ~5.7 tCO2e/person (2024, DERIVED: 47,944,551 tCO2e / ~8,478,000 residents; the last officially published per-capita figure is 6.2 t for 2023) — roughly 3x the benchmark, so clearly overshooting the ceiling. Moderated from Petaluma's 100 (7.25 t) because NYC's per-capita is 15-20% lower and the trend is genuinely downward: -25.2% against the 2005 baseline, with CY2024 the largest single-year cut in the 20-year series. The adversarial reviewer recommended 40 by scoring against the 40x30 target; the orchestrator overrode that under R12 because the Doughnut's outer ring measures planetary boundaries, not statutory compliance, and a 40 here would have shown NYC almost inside the doughnut beside Petaluma at 100 for near-identical per-capita emissions.
ecological.indicator: NYC Citywide Greenhouse Gas Emissions Inventory (production-based, Citywide-GPC/BASIC methodology, 100-yr GWP, per Local Law 22 of 2008)
ecological.value: 47.94 MtCO2e citywide in 2024 (exact: 47,944,551 tCO2e) — down 25.2% from the 2005 baseline of 64.14 MtCO2e (64,139,721 tCO2e) and down 4.9% from 2023's 50.43 MtCO2e (50,433,720 tCO2e), the largest single-year reduction in the 20-year series. Per capita: MOCEJ's most recently published figure is 6.2 tCO2e/person (2023), which MOCEJ notes is 'over 50% lower than the 2020 U.S. average of 13 tCO2e per capita'; a CY2024 per-capita figure has not yet been published, and 47.94 Mt over the Census Bureau's Vintage-2024 July-2024 city population of 8,478,000 implies roughly 5.7 tCO2e/person (DERIVED here, not an official MOCEJ figure). Exact CY2024 sector shares: Stationary Energy (buildings) 69.5%, Transportation 26.3%, Waste 4.2%. (CY2023 for comparison: 71.2% / 24.9% / 3.9%; MOCEJ's own rounded slide labels for 2023 were 72%/25%/4%, which sum to 101%.)
ecological.target: Local Law 22 of 2008 mandates the Citywide-GPC inventory that tracks Local Law 97/PlaNYC goals: 40% reduction below 2005 levels by 2030 (MOCEJ slide: 'Carbon Reduction Targets: Citywide: 40% by 2030'), and carbon neutrality by 2050. NY State's CLCPA sets a parallel but distinct target (40% below 1990 by 2030, 85% by 2050, 70% renewable electricity by 2030), tracked via a separate 'Citywide-CLCPA' inventory that additionally counts fugitive energy-related emissions and uses a 20-yr GWP to highlight methane's near-term warming — carried as a subIndicator below, not averaged into the headline.
ecological.context:
⚠ Citywide figure shown — not specific to Brooklyn. Not published; see Bronx note. Consumption-based CBEI proxy (different basis): Brooklyn = 11 tCO2e/person (2019).

At 47.9 MtCO2e total, NYC's absolute footprint is roughly 110x Petaluma's (~0.435 MtCO2e) on about 141x the population, and its production-based per-capita figure of 6.2 tCO2e (2023, MOCEJ-published) is genuinely LOWER than Petaluma's 7.25 tCO2e/person (2024) — a real, counter-intuitive result driven by density, transit ridership, and small, efficient housing units. The policy lever is different in kind from a small city's: Local Law 97 imposes binding, penalty-backed emissions caps on nearly 50,000 covered properties, holding about 60% of the city's building floor area and about 50% of building-sector emissions (roughly 35% of citywide emissions), enforced property-by-property rather than through a single utility or fleet decision. The major recent complication is the April 2021 closure of the Indian Point nuclear plant, which MOCEJ's own analysis shows increased in-city fossil generation and grid carbon intensity (289.6 to 369.9 kg CO2/MWh, 2019-2023; renewables share of NYC's grid 36% to 14%; share of grid served by in-city plants 47% to 59%) and concentrated the resulting pollution increase in disadvantaged waterfront neighborhoods. MOCEJ also reports NYC as the second-largest total emitter among C40 cities, with its production-based per-capita emissions ranking 'just above average' among C40 members.
ecological.source: NYC Open Data, 'NYC Greenhouse Gas Emissions Inventory' (dataset wq7q-htne, MOCEJ, updated 2025-12-16, includes CY2024); per-capita and reduction figures from MOCEJ, 'NYC 2023 Greenhouse Gas Inventory Methodology'; grid, sector and trajectory analysis from MOCEJ's 'NYC Greenhouse Gas Inventory' presentation to the Climate Knowledge Exchange, January 13, 2025
actions: If you sit on a co-op/condo board or manage a building over 25,000 sq ft, check your property's Local Law 97 filing status on NYC DOB's public compliance data and start a decarbonization plan now — Urban Green Council estimates 57% of covered properties already exceed the 2030 cap, and the penalty is $268 per metric ton over the limit.

Use NYC Accelerator (accelerator.nyc), the city's free technical-assistance program, to plan HVAC electrification retrofits, and look at the J51 tax abatement, which MOCEJ specifically flags as important for electrification projects to 'leapfrog' LL97 buildings off natural gas ahead of the 2030 caps.

Cut personal air travel and red-meat/dining-out consumption: per NYC's own Consumption-Based Emissions Inventory, air travel is 1.4 tCO2e per household — 34% of the average household's transportation footprint — and eating out plus animal products are nearly half of food emissions, which are themselves the single largest consumption category at 25% of the household total.

Push City Council and the Mamdani administration (in office since January 1, 2026) to fund LL97 enforcement and audits, protect the 2030 caps from weakening amendments, and advance large-scale renewable transmission (Champlain Hudson Power Express, offshore wind) — MOCEJ attributes 35% of the city's projected 2030 emissions progress to large-scale renewables, and project cancellations are the largest single risk to the target.

Support the Zero Waste Act's curbside organics program and use it consistently — MOCEJ lists landfilled waste as remaining constant even as wastewater-treatment efficiency has improved, and waste is 4.2% of citywide emissions.

If you live in a high-footprint tract — the CBEI's highest-emitting census tract is at 58 tCO2e/household against a citywide average of 29 and a lowest-tract figure of 18, a roughly 3-fold spread — prioritize reducing car ownership/VMT and air travel first. These are the categories where NYC households diverge most from a 1.5C-aligned per-capita budget, and the CBEI model identifies vehicle ownership and home size, not income alone, as the dominant drivers.
