global.levelRationale: NYC's own Consumption-Based Emissions Inventory puts residents' household consumption emissions at 11 tCO2e/person (2019) — roughly 5.5x to 6.9x the ~1.6-2.0 tCO2e/person range DEAL cites as 1.5C-aligned, which is the benchmark this portrait scores the global lens against. That 11 t is a FLOOR, not a full account: the CBEI's own Appendix 4 states that government and institutional consumption, if allocated to households, would add 5.5 tCO2e per household (17.66 MtCO2e citywide, about +2.2 t/person, taking the figure to roughly 13 t); the inventory also excludes business and tourism consumption entirely and predates the post-Indian-Point grid deterioration. The trend is close to flat — down only 7.7% across 2007-2019 — against C40's finding that high-income cities must cut consumption emissions by two-thirds within a decade. Scored above 100 for cross-portrait consistency: the Petaluma portrait scores 100 at an overshoot of 3.6-4.5x the same benchmark, and NYC's consumption overshoot is roughly 1.5x larger, so an identical 100 would flatten a real difference. Held below 150 ('severe/emergency') because 11 tCO2e/person is about two-thirds of the US household average of 17 and is falling, if far too slowly, so the top of the scale stays reserved for footprints that are worst-in-class or rising.
global.indicator: NYC Household Consumption-Based Emissions Inventory (CBEI) — lifecycle/scope-3 emissions from NYC residents' household consumption of food, goods, housing, services and private transport, wherever in the world those emissions physically occur
global.value: 92 million MTCO2e for NYC household consumption in 2019 across 3,211,033 households — about 29 MTCO2e per household, or about 11 MTCO2e per person. SCOPE: household consumption by NYC residents only; the CBEI excludes business and tourism consumption, non-residential building energy, and government/institutional consumption. Category breakdown per household: Food 7.5 t (25% of the total; eating out 1.7 t and animal products 1.8 t, each about 23% of food emissions), Housing 7.0 t (natural gas 3.7 t, about 53% and the largest single component), Services 5.9 t (healthcare 3.4 t, 57%), Goods 4.2 t (furnishings and appliances 1.6 t, 38%), Private transportation 4.1 t (air travel alone 1.4 t, 34% of the transport share). Personal air travel citywide therefore totals roughly 4.5 million MTCO2e/year (DERIVED: 1.4 t/household x 3.21 million households) — and this captures only NYC residents' personal flights, not the far larger throughput of non-resident passengers transiting JFK/LaGuardia/Newark, which is not attributable to the city under this method. Emissions vary roughly 3-fold between census tracts: 58 tCO2e/household in the highest-emitting tract against 18 in the lowest, with the citywide average at 29.
global.target: DEAL's 1.5C-aligned per-capita consumption benchmark of roughly 1.6-2.0 tCO2e/person — the portrait's standing benchmark, used so severity is comparable across dimensions and across the Petaluma and NYC portraits. CONTEXT ONLY, NOT AN NYC TARGET: C40's 'The Future of Urban Consumption in a 1.5C World' (2019) Table 1 gives per-capita consumption trajectory figures for the 'North America, Oceania & High Income Asia' typology of 15.6 tCO2e/capita in 2017, 5.9 by 2030 and 0.7 by 2050. That is a REGIONAL-TYPOLOGY AVERAGE across the 21 cities C40 grouped into NYC's typology (Austin, Auckland, Boston, Chicago, Hong Kong, Houston, Los Angeles, Melbourne, Montreal, New Orleans, New York, Philadelphia, Portland, San Francisco, Seattle, Seoul, Sydney, Tokyo, Toronto, Vancouver, Washington), not a New York City commitment, and must never be presented as one. C40's qualitative requirement for this group is that 'high-income cities must decrease by two thirds within the next decade.'
global.context: This is the single most important entry in NYC's ecological portrait: it is the number that shows the small-city framing fails for a global megacity. THE FINDING, stated so it does not depend on a ratio: NYC residents' household consumption alone drives 92 MtCO2e/yr — 11 tCO2e per person — and the great majority of those emissions occur outside the five boroughs, entirely invisible to the territorial inventory that Local Law 97 and the 40x30 target are tracked against. MOCEJ puts it plainly: 'the vast majority of goods and services consumed in New York City are produced elsewhere. This means that most emissions in the CBEI are scope 3.' C40 quantifies the same channel network-wide: 85% of the emissions associated with goods and services consumed in C40 cities are generated outside the city — 60% elsewhere in the same country and 25% abroad. THE 67% COMPARISON, WITH ITS CAVEAT: the CBEI's own conclusion is that 92 MtCO2e is 'about 67% more than in the territorial inventory' (which it states as 55 MtCO2e for 2019), and that 'a CBEI that is much larger than a territorial inventory indicates that New York City is a net exporter of emissions.' Quote that as the source's own framing, with three qualifications. First, the two accountings are not a partition of the same universe: the CBEI counts only resident household consumption while the territorial inventory counts all in-boundary activity including commercial, industrial and freight, so the comparison is directional evidence rather than an arithmetic difference. Second, MOCEJ's own integration paper is explicit that the two inventories 'are developed using very different methods that are not directly compatible', and combining them into an Integrated Inventory required an estimated overlap correction — roughly 17 million MTCO2e of residential energy use is common to both. They must not be summed or subtracted. Third, the 55 MtCO2e territorial figure is a superseded vintage: the current NYC Open Data series puts CY2019 Citywide-GPC at 52.69 MtCO2e, against which 92 Mt is 75% larger. The cleanest single sentence for citation: NYC residents' household consumption footprint of 11 tCO2e/person is roughly 1.8x the entire city's territorial footprint per resident (about 6.3 tCO2e/person in 2019), even though the household figure counts only households. TRANSMISSION MECHANISMS: trade (food, goods, construction materials), personal aviation, institutional procurement, and finance — NYC-headquartered banks underwriting fossil-fuel projects worldwide, a separate channel the consumption inventory does not cover and which remains unquantified here. POLICY LEVER: categorically different from Local Law 97 — consumer behaviour, supply-chain standards such as the Good Food Purchasing Program, and national/global production decarbonisation NYC cannot mandate. C40's modelling credits city governments and urban stakeholders with delivering 35% of the necessary reductions on their own, and finds that meeting Deadline 2020 production-based commitments alone addresses the ~25% of consumption emissions that overlaps the territorial inventory and closes 80% of the consumption gap; the remainder depends on the carbon intensity of production worldwide.
global.source: NYC Household Consumption-Based Emissions Inventory (EcoDataLab with C40 Cities and MOCEJ, funded by American Express), 2019 base year, published February 2023; methodological relationship to the territorial inventory from MOCEJ, 'Integrating New York City's 2019 Citywide and Consumption Based Greenhouse Gas Emissions Inventories'; global transmission figures from C40, 'The Future of Urban Consumption in a 1.5C World' (2019)

manhattan.note: Manhattan's per-household total of 27 tCO2e is the second-LOWEST of the five boroughs, below both Queens (33) and Brooklyn (28); its high per-capita figure is a household-size effect, since Manhattan has the smallest average household size in the city (27 t spread across roughly 2.1 people). global.boroughsNote: The borough ranking is NOT a simple affluence gradient and should not be described as one: Staten Island is highest and the Bronx lowest, while Manhattan — the highest-income borough — sits mid-table on a per-household basis. This is real, not an artefact. The CBEI model scales national expenditure data on six household characteristics — household size, income, VEHICLE OWNERSHIP, HOME SIZE, educational attainment and home ownership — so car ownership and detached-housing floor area pull as hard as income. That is why the car-dependent, single-family outer borough tops the table and the transit-dependent, small-apartment inner borough sits at the bottom. Note also that per-capita and per-household rankings differ because household size varies: Manhattan ranks 4th of 5 per household but 2nd per capita.

policyAnchors.name: Local Law 97 of 2019
policyAnchors.relevance: Binding, penalty-backed building emissions caps on nearly 50,000 covered properties (buildings over 25,000 gross sq ft, plus multi-building tax lots and condo boards over 50,000 sq ft), holding about 60% of NYC's building floor area and about 50% of building-sector emissions — roughly 35% of citywide emissions. A 2024-2029 compliance period is followed by a much tighter 2030-2034 cap; penalty is $268 per metric ton over the limit.
policyAnchors.status: First compliance-period reports (calendar year 2024) were due Dec 31, 2025. Per DOB's April 22, 2026 release, approximately 93% of covered privately owned properties, representing 91% of covered buildings, filed; roughly 1,400 properties failed to file and received Notices of Deficiency. DOB is still auditing the filings and has NOT yet published cap-compliance rates — it says it will do so later in 2026. Urban Green Council's independent modelling from CY2024 benchmarking data estimates about 9% of properties exceed their 2024-2029 cap but about 57% already exceed the 2030 cap. CY2025 reports are due May 1, 2026 and annually thereafter, with a grace period through June 30.

policyAnchors.name: Local Law 22 of 2008
policyAnchors.relevance: Establishes NYC's mandatory citywide GHG inventory (the source of the 'local' figures in this dossier) and requires it to track Local Law 97 goals. MOCEJ maintains four inventories under and alongside it: City Government, Citywide-GPC, Citywide-CLCPA, and Integrated Citywide & Consumption.
policyAnchors.status: Actively maintained by MOCEJ; 20 years of continuous data (2005-2024). The CY2024 inventory was published in December 2025 and the NYC Open Data dataset (wq7q-htne) was updated 2025-12-16.

policyAnchors.name: 40% below 2005 by 2030 and carbon neutrality by 2050
policyAnchors.relevance: The city's overarching production-based targets, tracked via the Citywide-GPC inventory. MOCEJ's charts contrast a business-as-usual trajectory (-51% by 2050) with a Climate Budgeting trajectory (-74%) and a Carbon Neutral trajectory.
policyAnchors.status: As of the CY2024 inventory the city is 25.2% below 2005, having cut 4.9% in a single year — the largest annual reduction in the series. MOCEJ's January 2025 presentation (on the CY2023 inventory, then at -20%) stated the city 'must more than double year-over-year reductions'; on the CY2024 basis the required pace is roughly 1.85x the 2005-2024 average. MOCEJ attributes 35% of projected 2030 progress to large-scale renewables and flags project cancellations as the principal risk.

policyAnchors.name: NY State Climate Leadership and Community Protection Act (CLCPA)
policyAnchors.relevance: State-level targets (40% below 1990 by 2030, 85% by 2050, 70% renewable electricity by 2030) that NYC tracks via a separate Citywide-CLCPA inventory methodology covering all Citywide-GPC sources plus fugitive energy-related emissions, and applying a 20-year GWP to highlight methane's near-term warming.
policyAnchors.status: The CLCPA-aligned inventory is confirmed to exist and is maintained alongside the GPC inventory; its figures are published in the same NYC Open Data dataset (2005 = 97.17 MtCO2e, 2024 = 78.74 MtCO2e, -19.0%). ecological.comparisonNote: Counter-intuitively, NYC's production-based per-capita footprint (6.2 tCO2e/person, 2023, MOCEJ-published; roughly 5.7 derived for 2024) is LOWER than Petaluma's 7.25 tCO2e/person (2024), driven by density, transit ridership and small, efficient housing — even though NYC's absolute emissions of 47.9 MtCO2e (2024) are roughly 110x Petaluma's ~0.435 MtCO2e on about 141x the population. Note that the two portraits score this dimension against different targets: Petaluma's local level is set against the DEAL 1.6-2.0 tCO2e/person benchmark, whereas NYC's local level is set against NYC's own statutory 40%-below-2005-by-2030 target, which is why the wedges differ more than the underlying per-capita figures do. NYC's consumption-based footprint (11 tCO2e/person, 2019) is where the comparison genuinely flips: it captures the embodied carbon in everything the city imports and consumes, which a small-city inventory like Petaluma's does not attempt to measure at all. It is this global/consumption lens — not the production lens — where NYC's status as a global financial and consumption centre actually shows up.

ecological.name: nitrogen & phosphorus loading
ecological.levelRationale: Anchored on the headline: NYC discharges approximately 18 billion gallons a year of untreated combined sewage through 398 permitted CSO outfalls into a eutrophication- and pathogen-sensitive estuary, and the binding abatement commitment is only 1.67 billion gallons a year — roughly 9% of that load — on a deadline that has already slid from 2030 to December 2040 with a December 2045 backstop. Pushed up by three well-sourced shortfalls named individually: the Flushing Bay CSO control tunnel is now scheduled for construction completion in Q4 2053 at $3.42B (from $683M and 2035 in the approved LTCP); green/managed acreage stands at 2,062 acres against the ~8,000 acres implied by the 10%-of-impervious 2030 goal, and DEP missed the 1.5%-by-2015 and 4%-by-2020 application-rate milestones outright; and citywide WRRF effluent nitrogen is ~132,200 lb/day (~21,900 t N/yr, ~2.6 kg N/person/yr), roughly half of per-capita excreted nitrogen, meaning the city removes only about half the nitrogen it collects. Pulled down — but only as a modifier, per R12, not as the anchor — by three genuinely met nutrient targets: the Long Island Sound point-source load is 68% below the TMDL baseline against a 60% requirement (18,909 lb/day, 2025); Jamaica Bay WRRF nitrogen is ~17,100 lb/day against ~40,000 in early 2010, a ~57% cut against a >50% target; and harbor-wide summer dissolved oxygen has exceeded the NYS 5.0 mg/L standard every summer since the 1990s. Also pulled down modestly by DEP certifying its December 2025 consent-order milestone (668 MGY of CSO reduction, $1.4B encumbered) on time, on 30 December 2025. Not scored lower because meeting one's own consent order is not the same as living within planetary means: nitrogen is among the most-transgressed planetary boundaries (~190 Tg N/yr against a 62 Tg boundary), and a chronic multi-billion-gallon untreated discharge with a 2053 fix date is not inside the safe space.
ecological.indicator: Combined sewer overflow (CSO) annual discharge volume
ecological.value: Approximately 18 billion gallons of combined sewage discharged citywide per year through 398 permitted CSO outfalls; approximately 60% of the city's sewer system is combined. This is NYSDEC's published modelled average-year estimate and carries no stated vintage; DEP's LTCP modelling is normalised to the 'average rainfall year of 2008' and DEP publishes no measured citywide annual total.
ecological.target: Reduce CSO volume by 1.67 billion gallons per year by December 2040 for the average rainfall year of 2008, with $3.5B in green infrastructure encumbered by December 2040 and expended by December 2045 (2023 Citywide Green Infrastructure Modification, DEC Case No. CO2-20230228-38, effective 29 June 2023, modifying the 2005 CSO Order CO2-20000107-8). Interim milestones: 668 MGY / $1.4B encumbered by December 2025; 700-800 MGY / $1.8B by December 2030; 850-1,220 MGY / $2.8B by December 2035.
ecological.context:
⚠ Citywide figure shown — not specific to Brooklyn. No borough-level CSO volume is published. PROXIES, each measuring a different quantity than the headline: (1) the four Brooklyn WRRFs discharged CY2025 means of ~2,617 lb/day (26th Ward, NY0026212), ~8,108 (Coney Island, NY0026182), ~26,342 (Newtown Creek, NY0026204), ~14,633 (Owls Head, NY0026166) and ~4,801 (Red Hook, NY0027073) total nitrogen — nitrogen loads, not CSO volumes, and assigned by plant location: 26th Ward and Coney Island discharge to Jamaica Bay, which borders Queens as well, and Newtown Creek WRRF discharges to the East River. (2) The Gowanus Canal receives an estimated 659 million gallons/year of CSO under its approved LTCP baseline, which is modelled for the 2008 average/typical rainfall year. (3) The 26th Ward carbon-addition facility, completed in February 2012 at ~$2M, cut >3,000 lb/day of nitrogen, then about 10% of total Jamaica Bay loading. Note also that 26th Ward is in Significant/Category I Noncompliance on its permit, with 9 quarters of SNC and copper, TSS, silver and whole-effluent-toxicity exceedances — a chemical-pollution issue rather than a nutrient one, flagged for the chemical pollution dimension.

This is a wastewater-and-CSO story, not an agricultural-runoff story — the sharp structural contrast with Petaluma, where the same dimension is scored on groundwater nitrate near farms and septic systems. NYC's 14 water resource recovery facilities process about 1.3 billion gallons a day, and 12 of those 14 sewersheds are combined-sewered, containing 398-418 permitted CSO outfalls (DEC's current figure is 398; DEC's 2021 CSO Annual Report says 400 across the 12 combined sewersheds; the 2023 consent order itself recites 'approximately 418'; DEP's website's figure of 700 is a broader count of combined-sewer outfalls, not a superseded CSO count). Nitrogen and pathogen loading are therefore concentrated at engineered point sources tied to rain events, not diffuse land-based leaching. The nitrogen side of this dimension has genuinely succeeded: about $1.2B was spent between 1999 and 2022 upgrading 8 plants for biological nitrogen removal, and the Long Island Sound and Jamaica Bay nutrient targets are both met. The CSO side has not: ~$5.3B was spent on CSO and green infrastructure between 1995 and 2024 with ~$7.4B more programmed for 2025-2050, yet the committed reduction is only 1.67 BGY and the major grey projects run past mid-century. Caveat on the headline: DEP's 16 December 2025 Flushing Bay presentation shows an 'Untreated CSO Volume Reduction' graphic labelled 5.6 BGY (Baseline CSO & GI Program, $6.2B) and 3.5 BGY (LTCP CSO Program, $8.7B) which could not be reconciled with the 18 BGY figure from the extracted slide text; whether 18 BGY is a pre-programme baseline or a current modelled volume is unresolved.
ecological.source: NYSDEC 'New York City CSO Program' and statewide CSO pages (citing NYC DEP data); 2023 Citywide Green Infrastructure Order on Consent (DEC Case No. CO2-20230228-38); NYC DEP 'State of the Sewers 2024'
actions: Sign up for NYC DEP's Sewage Pollution Right to Know Act discharge notifications before swimming, boating or fishing in the Gowanus Canal, Newtown Creek, Flushing Bay or Jamaica Bay — and hold DEP to the June 2026 Appellate Division ruling that its current advisories do not satisfy the four-hour notification requirement.

Comment during the Citywide (East River/Open Waters) and Jamaica Bay Long Term Control Plan public review processes (ltcp@dep.nyc.gov), and specifically on DEP's pending Flushing Bay modification request, which would push the CSO control tunnel's completion to Q4 2053.

Volunteer with Jamaica Bay Ecowatchers or the NY-NJ Harbor & Estuary Program on salt-marsh monitoring and restoration tied to the bay's nitrogen-loading history and the ribbed-mussel and basin-dredging work now underway under the CSO order.

Support DEP's transition to 100% beneficial reuse of biosolids by 2030 rather than landfilling, by following and commenting on DEP's Biosolids Beneficial Use Plan solicitations — this is the city's only live lever on phosphorus recovery, and it currently stands at roughly 31%.

Track and testify at the NYC Council Committee on Environmental Protection, Resiliency and Waterfronts on CSO-reduction reporting and green infrastructure funding, including the Council's own May 2025 finding that DEP's green infrastructure volume data is not published on NYC Open Data.

Cut household contributions to nutrient loads reaching CSO-affected waterways: keep lawn and garden fertiliser off paved surfaces and away from catch basins before rain, keep fats/oils/grease out of drains, and use the city's curbside organics collection so food waste is composted rather than adding nitrogen load at the treatment plant.

global.levelRationale: Now anchored on published quantities rather than on directional judgement, which is what R2 requires. Anthropogenic nitrogen fixation stands at roughly 190 Tg N/year against a planetary boundary of 62 Tg N/year — a ~3.1x global overshoot, making biogeochemical flows one of the most transgressed boundaries. An equal-per-capita share of the 62 Tg boundary across ~8.1 billion people is ~7.7 kg N/person/year. Published per-capita footprints for the relevant population are 41 kg N/person/year for the US average (Leach et al. 2012, N-Calculator; of which ~30 kg is food production) and 30 kg N/person/year for Baltimore City, the closest published US municipal analysis. NYC residents therefore sit at roughly 3.9x to 5.3x their per-capita share — clearly beyond 'critical', below the ~5.5-6.9x overshoot that puts the climate global lens at 120. Confidence is medium, not high: no NYC-specific nitrogen footprint study exists, the transfer of a Baltimore/US per-capita figure to NYC is an extrapolation, and the equal-per-capita downscaling of the boundary is reviewer arithmetic on published numbers rather than a published benchmark. The score is not higher because a dense city with no agriculture, near-universal sewer connection and partial biological nutrient removal plausibly sits at the lower end of the US range; it is not lower because every credible per-capita figure for a US urban population is multiples of the fair share.
global.indicator: NYC residents' embodied/consumption-based nitrogen footprint, benchmarked against an equal-per-capita share of the planetary nitrogen boundary; with the US consumer phosphorus footprint as the phosphorus counterpart
global.value: No NYC-specific study exists. Best available anchors: US average per-capita nitrogen footprint 41 kg N/person/year, of which food production is ~30 kg (Leach et al. 2012, N-Calculator/N-Print). Baltimore City community nitrogen footprint 30 kg N/person/year, ~19,000 metric tons N total in 2016, 73% from food production — the closest published US municipal-scale analysis. US consumer phosphorus footprint 4.4 kg P/person/year, against a food-portion nitrogen footprint of 22.4 kg N/person/year, i.e. ~5.2 kg N released per kg P (Metson/Leach et al., Environ. Res. Lett. 2020). Applying the 30-41 kg N/person/year range to ~8.26M residents implies an order-of-magnitude footprint of roughly 250,000-340,000 metric tons N/year, and the 4.4 kg P figure implies roughly 36,000 metric tons P/year — both explicitly extrapolations from non-NYC per-capita figures, not measured NYC quantities.
global.target: No NYC-specific target exists. Planetary anchor: the biogeochemical flows boundary sets anthropogenic nitrogen fixation at 62 Tg N/year against a current value of ~190 Tg N/year, and the regional phosphorus flow boundary at 6.2 Tg P/year against ~18.2 Tg P/year (Planetary Health Check, after Richardson et al. 2023; Steffen et al. 2015 gave the same 62 Tg N boundary). An equal-per-capita share of the 62 Tg N boundary is ~7.7 kg N/person/year — reviewer-derived from the published boundary and world population, not a published downscaled benchmark.
global.context: NYC's nitrogen and phosphorus footprint is transmitted globally through its food system: importing produce, grain, meat and dairy from farms using synthetic nitrogen fertiliser manufactured from fossil gas and phosphate fertiliser from mined rock, a finite resource heavily concentrated in Morocco/Western Sahara. Roughly 19 billion pounds of food pass through the city each year, and household food consumption accounts for about 20% of the city's consumption-based greenhouse gas footprint — the same import dependence that drives the nitrogen footprint. The Baltimore City analysis (Environ. Res. Lett. 2020) shows this accounting is feasible at municipal scale and that the dominant term is food production (73%), with energy and transport a combined 15%; it also found substantial variation across census block groups driven by income and development, which is the equity handle for NYC. On the phosphorus side, the return loop is broken: DEP produces approximately 1,300 wet tons of dewatered biosolids a day (~475,000 wet tons/year) across its 14 WRRFs, was landfilling 100% as of 2010, and currently beneficially uses roughly 31% against a stated goal of diverting 100% from landfill by 2030. Every ton landfilled rather than land-applied is phosphorus not returned to agricultural soil, against a finite global phosphate-rock reserve. No NYC phosphorus-recovery programme (struvite precipitation or equivalent) was identified in any source consulted, so the recovery framing is real in principle but unquantified and unimplemented here.
global.source: Planetary Health Check / Richardson et al. 2023 (boundary values); Leach et al. 2012 N-Calculator (US per-capita N footprint); Deemer/Wang et al., 'A community nitrogen footprint analysis of Baltimore City, Maryland', Environ. Res. Lett. 15 075007 (2020); Metson/Leach et al., 'The U.S. consumer phosphorus footprint', Environ. Res. Lett. (2020); NEBRA reporting on NYC DEP biosolids (Mar 2024)

policyAnchors.name: 2023 Citywide Green Infrastructure Modification to the CSO Order on Consent (DEC Case No. CO2-20230228-38, effective 29 June 2023, modifying CO2-20000107-8)
policyAnchors.relevance: Sets the binding citywide CSO reduction target (1.67 billion gallons/year by December 2040 for the average rainfall year of 2008, combined sewer areas only, no MS4 credit) and the green infrastructure funding schedule ($1.4B encumbered by Dec 2025, $1.8B by Dec 2030, $2.8B by Dec 2035, $3.5B encumbered by Dec 2040, $3.5B expended by Dec 2045), with matching interim CSO volume milestones of 668 MGY, 700-800 MGY and 850-1,220 MGY. It replaced the 2012 order's impervious-acre application-rate milestones, which the city had missed at both 1.5% (2015) and 4% (2020). Quarterly progress reporting continues under the 2012 order's case number, CO2-20110512-25.
policyAnchors.status: Active. DEP certified the December 2025 milestone complete on 30 December 2025 (668 MGY, $1.4B encumbered); DEC issued comments in January 2026, DEP responded in March 2026, and DEC review remained open as of the Q1 2026 quarterly report published 30 April 2026. Major capital projects are moving: the Newtown Creek CSO Storage Tunnel FEIS Notice of Completion issued 5 February 2026, City Council approved property acquisition 26 March 2026, and ULURP completed 6 April 2026. The Flushing Bay modification request (6.5 MG in-line storage plus a 40 MG tunnel, $3.42B, completion Q2 2037 and Q4 2053) was submitted 31 December 2025 and is under DEC review; DEP told DEC it needed guidance before the end of May 2026 to proceed with in-line storage design.

policyAnchors.name: Sewage Pollution Right to Know Act (SPRTKA) enforcement — Matter of Riverkeeper v NYC DEP
policyAnchors.relevance: SPRTKA requires public notification of combined sewer overflow discharges within four hours; how fast residents learn of nitrogen- and pathogen-bearing discharges determines whether the CSO load translates into human exposure at the Gowanus Canal, Newtown Creek, Flushing Bay and Jamaica Bay.
policyAnchors.status: Resolved against DEP and affirmed on appeal. The Supreme Court ruled in December 2023 that DEP had failed to notify the public as SPRTKA requires; the Appellate Division, Second Department affirmed in June 2026 (Matter of Riverkeeper, Inc. v New York City Dept. of Envtl. Protection, 2026 NY Slip Op 03444), granting mandamus to compel prompt public notification of untreated and partially untreated sewage discharges and holding that DEP's water quality advisories in their current form do not comply with SPRTKA. Petitioners were represented by the Pace Environmental Litigation Clinic on behalf of Riverkeeper, Save the Sound, Bronx Council for Environmental Quality, Newtown Creek Alliance, the NYC Water Trail Association, NY/NJ Baykeeper and Waterkeeper Alliance. Confidence medium: the slip opinion itself is not machine-fetchable and this rests on the reported citation and summary.

policyAnchors.name: Long Island Sound Nitrogen TMDL (2000 TMDL, EPA-approved 2001)
policyAnchors.relevance: The binding regional nutrient target NYC's East River WRRF upgrades were built to satisfy: a 60% reduction in point-source nitrogen from a baseline of 59,000 trade-equalized lb/day.
policyAnchors.status: Point-source target met and exceeded. The combined New York and Connecticut point-source load was 18,909 lb/day in 2025, a 68% reduction from baseline; the 60% goal was first met in 2016 and loads have continued to fall. Hypoxic area and volume in the Sound are trending down. Implementation continues under EPA's 2015 Nitrogen Reduction Strategy and New York's Long Island Nitrogen Action Plan (2015), and ecosystem-level targets such as eelgrass extent remain below goals — so the nutrient-loading requirement is complete while ecological recovery is not.

policyAnchors.name: 2010 Jamaica Bay Nitrogen Consent Agreement
policyAnchors.relevance: The $115M agreement (~$100M in WRRF nitrogen-control technology plus ~$15M for marsh restoration) that drove the Jamaica Bay nitrogen cuts, targeting a reduction of more than 50% over ten years from approximately 40,000 lb/day in early 2010.
policyAnchors.status: Target met. The four Jamaica Bay WRRFs averaged ~17,100 lb/day of total nitrogen in CY2025 per their own discharge monitoring reports, a ~57% reduction from the 2010 baseline. Component projects were delivered over 2012-2020: the 26th Ward carbon-addition facility (February 2012, >3,000 lb/day), $460M in upgrades at Jamaica and 26th Ward, and a $23M Rockaway upgrade (2018). Marsh and habitat work continues under the CSO order — ribbed mussel installation in Thurston Basin and Bergen Basin dredging certified design start in February 2026, and Spring Creek CSO facility tide gates entered full operation on 22 September 2025.

policyAnchors.name: NYS Clean Water, Clean Air and Green Jobs Environmental Bond Act (2022, $4.2B)
policyAnchors.relevance: A funding source explicitly eligible for CSO, stormwater and water-infrastructure projects (at least $200M for water infrastructure and at least $250M for stormwater and algal-bloom-related projects statewide), relevant to financing the $3.5B green infrastructure commitment.
policyAnchors.status: Passed by referendum in 2022; grant guideline documents were still being issued and revised into 2024, and the NY League of Conservation Voters published a 'three years on' status review. Implementation is ongoing rather than complete.

policyAnchors.name: NYC DEP Biosolids Beneficial Use Plan and 100%-landfill-diversion goal
policyAnchors.relevance: The phosphorus return loop: ~1,300 wet tons/day of biosolids, 100% landfilled as of 2010, currently ~31% beneficially used, against a goal of diverting 100% from landfill to beneficial use by 2030. Determines whether phosphorus collected from the city's food supply is returned to soil or buried.
policyAnchors.status: Active but well short of the goal; DEP has been soliciting beneficial-use partners. No NYC phosphorus-recovery (e.g. struvite) facility was identified. Current-year destination and landfill-versus-beneficial-use percentages could not be confirmed from a 2025/2026 primary DEP publication.

ecological.comparisonNote: Petaluma's nitrogen and phosphorus story is groundwater nitrate near agricultural land and septic systems (most wells below the 10 mg/L drinking-water standard, with 4-7 mg/L hotspots near agricultural boundaries, scored level 20). NYC's is an engineered wastewater-and-CSO story roughly three orders of magnitude larger: approximately 18 billion gallons a year of combined sewage through 398 permitted outfalls, and 14 WRRFs discharging some 132,200 lb/day of total nitrogen (~21,900 t N/year) into an estuarine system. There is essentially no diffuse agricultural-runoff analog in NYC's version of this dimension, and no groundwater-nitrate analog either, since the city draws its water from upstate reservoirs rather than local wells. The structural difference cuts both ways: NYC's loading is concentrated at monitored point sources, which is why it has been cut by 57-68% under two enforceable nutrient targets that have both been met — a lever Petaluma's diffuse problem does not offer — while NYC's untreated wet-weather discharge has no Petaluma counterpart at all and is on a fix timeline running to 2053.
dataGaps: DEP and DEC publish no rolled-up citywide nitrogen (or phosphorus) loading total across the 14 WRRFs. This review built one from EPA ECHO discharge monitoring reports (~132,200 lb/day, CY2025), but it is a reviewer-computed unweighted mean of monthly averages, not a flow-weighted annual load and not an agency figure. NYC DEP's Bureau of Wastewater Treatment or NYSDEC's eDMR system holds the underlying data needed to do this properly.

The ~18 billion gallons/year headline carries no stated vintage. NYSDEC publishes it as an average with no year; DEP publishes no measured citywide annual total and normalises all LTCP modelling to the 'average rainfall year of 2008'. Competing figures do not reconcile: the State Comptroller reported 6.5 billion gallons of partially or untreated wastewater in FY2016-17, Riverkeeper's SPRTKA filings use 21 billion gallons through 460 outfalls, and Save the Sound uses 27 billion gallons. Most importantly, DEP's own 16 December 2025 Flushing Bay presentation shows an 'Untreated CSO Volume Reduction' graphic labelled 5.6 BGY (Baseline CSO & GI Program) and 3.5 BGY (LTCP CSO Program) that could not be reconciled with an 18 BGY total from the extracted slide text. Whether 18 BGY is a pre-programme baseline or a current modelled volume is unresolved and materially affects the level.

The outfall count needs a stated definition, not just a number. NYSDEC currently says 398 permitted CSO outfalls; its 2021 CSO Annual Report says 400 across the 12 of 14 WRRF sewersheds that are combined; the 2023 consent order recites 'approximately 418'; DEP's website says 700 combined sewer outfalls; advocacy filings use 460. These are different measures, not successive revisions.

No borough-aggregated CSO volume totals are published. DEP and DEC report by waterbody or drainage area (Gowanus Canal, Newtown Creek, Flushing Bay, Flushing Creek, Jamaica Bay and Tributaries, Bronx River, Hutchinson River, Alley Creek, Coney Island Creek, Westchester Creek, East River/Open Waters), which only partially maps to boroughs and often spans two. Staten Island has no waterbody LTCP at all.

Current (2025/2026) biosolids destination and landfill-versus-beneficial-use percentages could not be confirmed from a primary DEP publication; the ~31% beneficial use / ~69% landfill split comes from 2024 reporting. The claim sometimes made that NYC historically land-applied biosolids out of state (Colorado, Florida, 1992-2010) could not be verified and has been removed. ecological.name: land conversion
ecological.levelRationale: 50 is defensible if and only if the dimension is scored purely as canopy-versus-goal, but it is too high once the target is stated accurately and the orchestrator's density ruling is applied. On the target: Local Law 148's 30% is statutory but carries NO deadline; 2040 is an administrative date chosen in April 2026 and 2035 was never in the law. So the sharpest negative available — 'the city has blown a legal deadline' — does not exist. What does exist: 23.4% is 78% of the way to the goal; canopy rose in all five boroughs 2017-2021 (+1.2 pts, ~+0.3 pts/yr); at that rate 30% arrives around 2043, and press analysis of the 2026 plan puts it at 2055 or later on current funding, with Comptroller Levine (April 2026) finding forested natural areas get ~0.7% of the Parks expense budget. Against that, on land conversion proper NYC is close to neutral-positive: the city is built out, its 2024 rezoning (City of Yes, 82,000 homes) adds capacity by infill rather than by extending the built footprint, per-capita land consumption is the lowest of major US cities (~459 m2/person), 14% of city land is NYC parkland, and the orchestrator has ruled the density is genuinely land-conserving at regional scale. The remaining genuine problems are a 7-point EJ canopy gap (19% vs 26%), net canopy loss on one- and two-family residential lots concentrated in southeastern Queens, and largely irreversible historic wetland loss (Jamaica Bay 2,350 acres of marsh islands in 1951 to ~800 today, only ~60 acres restored at Elders Point). That profile is worse than 'on track' (0) but well short of a full 'needs attention' (50): 25 is the honest placement. I flag for the orchestrator that this is a disagreement about indicator scope, not about any number — the canopy data and the borough data both survived verification intact.

Unlike Petaluma, where 'land conversion' means whether farmland/open space outside an urban growth boundary gets paved over, NYC is already ~72% impervious — the meaningful question is how much of the remaining pervious/natural fraction is protected, growing, or being lost, and whether the city's own growth model (infill density) is itself averting conversion elsewhere. Nearly 90% of 2017–2021 canopy growth came from existing trees expanding rather than new plantings, and the only net canopy LOSS citywide was on one- and two-family residential lots, concentrated in southeastern Queens — meaning small-lot residential development/hardscaping is the marginal driver of loss even in a built-out city. ecological.name: air pollution
ecological.levelRationale: The headline alone supports something close to 25: DOHMH's published citywide annual mean of 6.26 µg/m³ (2024) is 25% above the WHO 2021 guideline of 5 µg/m³, no NYC county is designated nonattainment for PM2.5, monitor design values run 7.7-8.3 against a 9.0 NAAQS, and the trend is strongly favourable (PM2.5 −36%, NO2 −41%, black carbon −56%, SO2 −98% since 2009). Per R1 the level must then be adjusted for well-sourced shortfalls inside the same dimension, and there are four material ones. (1) Ozone: all five boroughs sit in 'Serious' 2015-ozone-NAAQS nonattainment with an August 3, 2027 attainment deadline, and NYCCAS shows no downward ozone trend at all (24.3 ppb in 2009 to 32.3 ppb in 2024) with DOHMH expecting it to worsen with warming — a dimension cannot be 'mild' when the region formally fails a health standard and the failing pollutant is flat-to-rising. (2) Mortality and morbidity burden: DOHMH attributes ~2,000 excess deaths/yr (1 in 25 deaths citywide) to long-term PM2.5, with a modelled 1,798 deaths/yr age 30+ and 1,125 pediatric asthma ED visits/yr in the 2017-2019 vintage. (3) Distributional failure: child asthma ED visits range from 441.8 per 10,000 in Brownsville to 20.6 in Tottenville–Great Kills (2023), roughly 21x, and Manhattan's PM2.5 (7.71) is 30% above Queens's (5.95) with Midtown at 10.5 — the citywide mean conceals an exposure gradient the dimension exists to show. (4) Episodic overshoot: two severe wildfire-smoke events in three years (AQI 465 in June 2023, AQI 289 across five days in July 2026 alongside a heat emergency), and the 2023 citywide regulatory-monitor annual average of 10.8 µg/m³ exceeded the federal standard outright. On the other side, R5 forbids manufacturing a crisis: this is a city with a genuine multi-decade improvement record, the most granular urban monitoring network in the US, and a documented policy win in the residual-oil phase-out. 100 would be doom inflation and 25 launders the ozone failure and the mortality burden. 50 — 'needs attention' — is the honest reading. The global lens stays at 50: the outbound channels are now quantified (port share of county NOx up to 17.5%, the only tri-state monitor above the 9.0 NAAQS sitting inside the port complex at 9.4 µg/m³, and NY-source contributions above 14 ppb on Connecticut's worst ozone days), so R2's requirement for quantification is met and a score rather than null is justified.

NYC's PM2.5 story is fundamentally about intra-city gradient, not a single citywide number: the ~2x range from Rockaway (Queens, 5.3 µg/m³) to Midtown (Manhattan, 10.5 µg/m³) reflects traffic density, building-heating combustion, and street-canyon effects, not a uniform exposure. global.levelRationale: NYC cannot unilaterally control two of the three largest pressures on its air-pollution ceiling: (1) upwind/interstate ozone-precursor transport, part of why the NY-NJ-CT region was reclassified from 'Moderate' to 'Serious' 2015-ozone-NAAQS nonattainment in July 2024 despite the city's own local control measures, and (2) increasingly frequent transboundary Canadian wildfire smoke (2023, recurring 2024 and again mid-July 2026) that is itself a downstream effect of global climate change. Layered on top, the Port of NY/NJ — the busiest port on the US East Coast — services NYC-area (and much wider) consumption demand and its ocean-going vessels alone account for 53% of the port's NOx and 36% of its PM2.5 emissions, a footprint driven by global containerized trade rather than by New Yorkers' local combustion. 'Needs attention' reflects a real, evidenced overshoot with only partial local leverage, not an unquantified hand-wave.

global.context: NYC's air-pollution footprint is not a closed local system. Regionally, the metro area's persistent ozone problem is driven substantially by NOx and VOC transport from upwind states and the wider Ozone Transport Region, which is why New York, New Jersey, and Connecticut jointly petitioned for and received the 2024 'Serious' reclassification rather than fixing it through city-level action alone — this is the ozone-pollution analogue to a 'consumption-based' emissions argument in the climate dimension. Separately, the Port of NY/NJ exists to serve import/export demand — much of it NYC consumption — and its ocean-going vessels, drayage trucks, and cargo-handling equipment emit PM2.5 and NOx concentrated in South Bronx, Red Hook, and New Jersey waterfront communities that host the region's port and last-mile e-commerce warehouse infrastructure. And the escalating frequency of Canadian wildfire smoke intrusions (2023, 2024, and again mid-July 2026) means an increasing share of NYC's worst PM2.5 days now originates entirely outside city and even national jurisdiction, tied to boreal-forest climate change. Aviation (JFK, LaGuardia, Newark) is a further plausible contributor to both local NOx/PM near the airports and to NYC's share of global aviation emissions, but no single quantified 'NYC aviation air-pollution footprint' figure was located in this research pass.

ecological.name: waste & materials
ecological.levelRationale: Headline curbside & containerized diversion rate is 18.5% (FY2025), essentially flat against a multi-year historical band (FY2018: 18.0%, FY2021: 17.6%, FY2022: 17.0%, FY2025: 18.5% — SWMP26 Table 1-5 and FY2025 Zero Waste Report), against a stated 2030 zero-waste goal that DSNY itself now calls 'likely not attainable.' The city's own broader DSNY-Managed Diversion Rate (a more generous metric including voluntary/non-curbside diversion under Local Law 40 of 2010) reached 21.8% in FY2025, up from 20.6% in FY2024 — real improvement, but still far below any zero-waste trajectory. Organics capture rate (share of divertible organic material actually captured in the brown bin, per DSNY's Waste Characterization Study) is only 7.2% in FY2025, despite curbside organics now being mandatory citywide since 2024 — indicating a large compliance/participation gap on the single highest-leverage material stream (food waste is the largest fraction of NYC's residential waste stream). No active in-city landfill or waste-to-energy capacity exists since Fresh Kills closed in 2001; 100% of non-diverted residential and commercial waste is exported out of the five boroughs (truck, rail, or barge via Marine Transfer Stations) at a cost in the hundreds of millions of dollars annually, meaning NYC's entire non-diverted waste stream is displaced onto other jurisdictions' landfills and incinerators (mostly Pennsylvania, Ohio, Virginia, South Carolina) — a material scale of transmission that would be disqualifying on its own even before diversion performance is considered. Weighing (a) diversion essentially flat/stagnant against a stated 2030 goal now admitted to be unreachable, (b) very low organics capture despite a mandatory program, and (c) total dependency on waste export with no in-city end-of-life capacity, against (d) genuine incremental improvement in the broader DSNY-Managed rate and a real, functioning regulatory infrastructure (Zero Waste Act, Commercial Waste Zones, Waste Equity Law) actively working the problem, I score this 70 ('needs attention' trending toward 'critical') rather than higher — the system is moving, just too slowly relative to its own targets.

global.indicator: International/out-of-region material footprint of NYC's exported waste and recyclables — NOT QUANTIFIED
global.context: Per R2: a null score with strong qualitative framing is preferred over attaching an invented number. Two real, verified transmission channels exist but neither could be quantified to a hard figure from available primary or secondary sources: (1) INTERSTATE waste export — DSNY exports 100% of non-diverted waste (both residential and commercial) via truck, rail, and barge from Marine Transfer Stations to out-of-state landfills/incinerators, primarily in Pennsylvania, Ohio, Virginia, and South Carolina, at a cost of roughly $495M-$514M/year (FY2025, see local-lens subIndicators). This is technically an interstate rather than international transmission channel, so it is documented here as context rather than scored as the 'global' lens result — but it is a real displaced ecological/environmental-justice burden onto receiving-state communities that a full portrait should surface (receiving landfills' EJ demographics are documented in DSNY's Draft SWMP26 but not aggregated into a single footprint figure). (2) INTERNATIONAL recyclables market exposure — NYC's curbside recycling (processed largely at Sims Municipal Recycling's Sunset Park, Brooklyn facility, ~1,000 tons/day capacity) is sold into international commodity markets and has been structurally disrupted since China's 2018 'National Sword' policy banned most imported mixed paper and plastic scrap. Available sourcing describes materials as sold 'on the east coast and in Canada' with explicit acknowledgment that 'there are no buyers for plastic bags in the US' for some film/mixed-plastic streams — but no source found (DSNY, Sims, NYSDEC, or academic/NGO) publishes a quantified tonnage-by-destination-country breakdown or a consumption-based international material-footprint figure for NYC specifically. Rather than force a number onto this qualitative reality, this lens is scored null with the framing above. A materials-flow analysis by NYSDEC, Sims Municipal Recycling, or an academic/NGO materials-flow research group (e.g., Columbia University's Earth Institute, or the Natural Resources Defense Council's waste program) could plausibly quantify this in Phase 2.

ecological.comparisonNote: This is one of the sharpest structural contrasts in the whole portrait. NYC has had zero in-city landfill or waste-to-energy capacity since Fresh Kills closed in 2001; every ton of its non-diverted waste — residential and commercial — is exported out of the five boroughs by truck, rail, or barge at a cost of roughly half a billion dollars a year, displacing the ecological and environmental-justice burden onto receiving communities in Pennsylvania, Ohio, Virginia, and South Carolina. Petaluma, by contrast, sits within Sonoma County's own solid-waste system: the Sonoma County Central Landfill has an estimated 15-25 years of remaining in-county capacity, and Petaluma's curbside collection (residential + commercial, under an exclusive Recology Sonoma Marin franchise) includes mandatory organics/food-scrap collection under California's SB 1383 (effective Jan 1, 2022), with countertop kitchen pails provided to residents to ease participation. In other words: Petaluma disposes of its waste largely within a system it can still see and govern locally, while NYC's scale has forced it into permanent, costly, and equity-fraught exporter status. That said, the comparison should not be read as Petaluma having 'solved' waste — Petaluma's own Doughnut portrait (data/petaluma_ca.json) currently has NO filled-in waste & materials indicator at all ('Need more input from City' is the literal placeholder text), so no verified Petaluma-specific diversion rate exists yet for a true side-by-side number. Sonoma County-wide, roughly two-thirds of the ~262,500 tons disposed of annually is estimated to be divertible, potentially divertible, or compostable (Zero Waste Sonoma), suggesting a real diversion gap exists in Sonoma County too, just at a vastly smaller absolute and per-capita scale than NYC's, and without the export/environmental-justice dimension that defines NYC's system. Recommend that Amelia's team prioritize filling Petaluma's own waste-and-materials indicator (Zero Waste Sonoma's annual report and Recology Sonoma Marin are the logical next sources) so the contrast can eventually be stated in real, comparable diversion-rate numbers rather than structural description alone.

ecological.name: heat & climate resilience
ecological.levelRationale: BENCHMARK NOTE (R12): this is one of the two locally-defined ecological dimensions (R6). There is no Raworth planetary boundary for urban heat mortality and no DEAL downscaled per-capita benchmark, so R12's instruction to score against the framework benchmark has no direct analogue. The benchmark scored against is stated explicitly: ZERO PREVENTABLE HEAT DEATHS. That is the defensible framework-equivalent because DOHMH itself frames these deaths as preventable and the dominant risk factor is a purchasable good — home AC and the ability to run it — rather than an irreducible meteorological hazard; and unlike a city statute it applies identically to any portrait, which is R12's actual purpose. ANCHOR: ~500 heat-related deaths/year, about 3% of all warm-season deaths, heat being NYC's deadliest weather hazard, against a benchmark of zero. PUSHED UP BY (R1): the direct heat-stress racial disparity has WIDENED rather than closed in the current vintage — Black New Yorkers at 3x the white age-adjusted rate (1.2 vs 0.4 per million, 2016-2025) against 2x in the previous vintage — nine years after Cool Neighborhoods NYC (2017) made closing it an explicit aim; 2025 produced 21 heat-stress deaths, the highest single-year tally in over a decade, 19 of them in one four-day June heat wave, and 18 of the 21 decedents were Black or Latino; ~493,000 rental households have AC they do not run because of utility cost, so ownership statistics overstate real protection; the most heat-vulnerable neighbourhood citywide by HVI, East Flatbush (85% Black), has 1.2 cooling centres per 100,000 residents against Manhattan's 7.1. PULLED DOWN BY, but insufficient to move the score: citywide AC penetration of ~90-91% is genuinely high and is reported as such per R5; Local Law 128 of 2025 now makes a 7-per-100,000 cooling-centre target statutory with a plan due 15 May 2026; Local Law 41 of 2021 requires resilient design across the ~$90B city capital portfolio from 2026; CoolRoofs has coated more than 10M sq ft since 2009. Those are inputs, not outcomes, and the outcome measure has not improved. Not raised to 150 (emergency) because programmes exist and are expanding and the toll is not accelerating on a like-for-like basis. Level 100 (Critical) retained.
ecological.indicator: Heat-related mortality (direct heat-stress deaths + modelled heat-exacerbated deaths)
ecological.value: ~500 heat-related deaths per year citywide, May-September — about 3% of all warm-season deaths (2026 New York City Heat-Related Mortality Report, DOHMH, released 15 June 2026). This is a MULTI-YEAR ANNUAL AVERAGE, not a single-year count: an average of 7 direct heat-stress deaths/year (pooled 2016-2025) plus an average of ~490 modelled heat-exacerbated deaths/year (pooled 2014-2023), where heat aggravates an existing condition. EQUITY — SCOPE STATED PRECISELY: DOHMH's race-disaggregated rates cover DIRECT HEAT-STRESS DEATHS ONLY. For 2016-2025 the age-adjusted heat-stress death rate was 1.2 per million for Black New Yorkers and 1.0 for Latino New Yorkers against 0.4 for white New Yorkers — 3x and 2x respectively, in DOHMH's own words 'Black New Yorkers had heat-stress death rates three times higher and Latino New Yorkers had death rates two times higher than white New Yorkers.' DOHMH publishes NO race-disaggregated rate for the ~490/year heat-exacerbated component that makes up ~98% of the headline; for that component its inequity finding is qualitative ('inequitably affects Black New Yorkers, reflecting the impacts of structural racism'). The ratio and the headline therefore describe different populations and must not be conflated. Corroborating single-year fact: in 2025, 21 New Yorkers died of heat stress — the highest tally in over a decade, 19 of them during one four-day June heat wave — and 18 of the 21 were Black or Latino.
ecological.target: No codified numeric mortality target exists, and no planetary boundary applies to this locally-defined dimension. The benchmark used for scoring is ZERO PREVENTABLE HEAT DEATHS plus elimination of the racial disparity in heat mortality — the aim DOHMH and Cool Neighborhoods NYC (2017) state in qualitative terms, pursued via AC access and affordability, cooling centres, tree canopy and cool roofs. Statutory commitments that exist (Local Law 41 of 2021 on resilient capital design; Local Law 128 of 2025's 7-cooling-centres-per-100,000 target) are progress measures reported in context and policyAnchors, never the scoring anchor.
ecological.context:
⚠ Citywide figure shown — not specific to Brooklyn. PROXY ONLY — no borough-level heat-mortality rate is published, per R10. DOHMH's 2026 report names Brooklyn (with the Bronx) as having the highest age-adjusted heat-STRESS death rates, qualitatively and without a figure. Closest proxies, each measuring something other than the headline: HVI 5 in East Flatbush, Bedford-Stuyvesant, Brownsville, and East New York and Starrett City (a MODELLED VULNERABILITY COMPOSITE); and cooling-centre density — a FACILITY-SUPPLY measure, not a mortality outcome — where East Flatbush, 85% Black and the most underserved neighbourhood citywide, has 2 centres for 162,446 residents (1.2 per 100,000) against Bedford-Stuyvesant's 9 centres for 174,960 residents (5.1 per 100,000).

In an 8.3M-person city, heat kills more people annually than all other weather hazards combined, and the mechanism is overwhelmingly indoor and socioeconomic (un-air-conditioned homes, and AC that households cannot afford to run) rather than purely meteorological — sharply different from Petaluma's wildfire-smoke-centered climate-health narrative. VINTAGE LADDER (R11), all confirmed from primary sources: the 2022 report (released 16 June 2022) gave ~370 deaths/year with race rates for 2011-2020 (Black 2.2 vs white 0.9 per million, 2x); the 2025 report (released 30 June 2025) gave ~525/year pooled 2018-2022, of which ~5/year heat-stress and ~520/year heat-exacerbated, with race rates for 2014-2023 (Black 0.8 vs white 0.4, 2x); the 2026 report gives ~500/year with race rates for 2016-2025 (Black 1.2, Latino 1.0, white 0.4, i.e. 3x and 2x). The step from ~370 to ~500-525 is driven principally by a moved pooling window and by DOHMH's successive refinements to the heat-exacerbated excess-mortality model — it is a methodology and scope shift, NOT a measured trend, and the portrait must not read it as a rise; note the current ~500 is in fact BELOW the previous vintage's ~525. The widening of the Black:white direct heat-stress ratio from 2x to 3x reflects the June 2025 heat wave entering the pooling window. The policy lever is AC access and its affordability (utility cost, not just ownership), tree canopy in redlined/EJ neighborhoods, and building-level cooling requirements; Local Law 97's building-emissions caps and heat-pump retrofit push interact with this because electrified cooling raises electricity demand even as it cuts direct heat-stress risk.
ecological.source: NYC DOHMH, 2026 New York City Heat-Related Mortality Report (Environment & Health Data Portal data feature and the 15 June 2026 press release); prior vintages 2025 (30 June 2025) and 2022 (16 June 2022) reports for the comparison ladder
actions: Apply early for the NY State HEAP Cooling Assistance Benefit via ACCESS NYC or OTDA each spring — funds are first-come-first-served and the 2026 benefit closed on 5 June, so late applicants are shut out for the whole summer. Note you are ineligible if your household received a HEAP-funded AC within the past five years.

During a heat emergency, use NYC Emergency Management's Cooling Center Finder or call 311 to locate the nearest cooling center (library, community or senior center, or NYCHA facility) under the Local Law 85/128 network.

If you live in a basement or cellar apartment, check eligibility for the city's basement and cellar legalization pilot (Local Law 126 of 2024) through DOB/HPD before the 20 April 2029 deadline — but note flood-prone properties are excluded from the programme, so know your flood-evacuation route regardless, given the Hurricane Ida basement-death pattern.
Support or join the NYC Environmental Justice Alliance's (NYC-EJA) Extreme Heat & Air Quality campaign, which pushes for equitable cooling-center density and canopy investment in HVI-5 neighborhoods.

In the South Bronx, connect with or volunteer for the Be A Buddy program (run by The Point CDC in Hunts Point) which does neighbor check-ins for isolated, heat-vulnerable residents during extreme-heat days.

Hold NYCEM to Local Law 128 of 2025: the comprehensive cooling and communication plan was due on or before 15 May 2026 and the law sets a target of no fewer than 7 cooling centers per 100,000 residents — compare that against your own neighborhood's actual count.

Track your community board's Cloudburst/Stormwater Resiliency Plan timeline and the NY-NJ Harbor & Tributaries Study public comment process (Army Corps/DEP), since both determine whether and when your neighborhood gets flood infrastructure.
